metadata.title: Southwest Florida Plant Guide
metadata.description: Comprehensive plant reference guide for Southwest Florida covering native, beneficial non-native, edible, and invasive plants across 15 categories.
metadata.schema_notes: v3.0 adds family, plant_tier, scenarios, usda_zone, has_invasive_lookalike, hoa_friendly, pollinator_value, where_to_buy. Origin: beneficial_non_native → non_native_low_risk. beneficial_score: numeric → exceptional/good/limited.

new_tags.beneficial_score: 1-7 scale based on defined ecological criteria

plants.description: The single most ecologically important tree you can plant in SW Florida. Supports hundreds of caterpillar and moth species — critical food for nesting birds. Acorns feed squirrels, deer, turkeys, blue jays, and woodpeckers year-round. Massive spreading canopy provides prime nesting sites for eagles, owls, and songbirds. Long-lived, hurricane resistant, and deeply beautiful. Give it significant room — it spreads as wide as it is tall.
plants.growth_notes: Slow in first 1-2 years while establishing root system, then accelerates
plants.pruning_notes: Prune only dead or damaged wood. Never top a live oak — it permanently damages the tree and creates dangerous deadwood.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Once established, live oak is essentially indestructible in SW Florida. The challenge is patience — it takes years to establish.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Keystone species supporting hundreds of insect species, cavity nesters, acorn producers, and canopy habitat. Maximum ecological value.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect acorns when they fall naturally. Plant immediately — acorns lose viability quickly. Plant 1 inch deep in sandy soil.
plants.germination_notes: Plant fresh acorns immediately after collection — viability drops significantly after 2-4 weeks
plants.transplant_notes: Buy smallest available container size — live oaks transplant better when small. Stake for first year. Water deeply weekly for first full year regardless of rainfall.
do_not_plant_near: Structures, driveways, and utilities — spreading root system and canopy require significant space. Minimum 20 ft from any structure.
plants.looks_like_plants: Turkey oak (Quercus laevis), water oak (Quercus nigra)
plants.looks_like_notes: Other Florida oaks are similar but live oak is the only evergreen oak. The rounded lobed leaves and spreading horizontal canopy are distinctive.
plants.attracts_specific: Blue jay (primary acorn disperser), Red-headed woodpecker, Pileated woodpecker (cavity), Great horned owl (nesting), Eastern screech owl, Hundreds of Lepidoptera species as host plant

seasonal_care.january: No action needed. Brief leaf drop and replacement happens now.
seasonal_care.february: Light leaf drop continues — normal, not a disease. Do not rake aggressively.
seasonal_care.march: New leaf flush. Best time for any necessary structural pruning.
seasonal_care.april: Full canopy established. No action needed.
seasonal_care.may: Monitor for oak galls — unsightly but not harmful, no treatment needed.
seasonal_care.july: Monitor for any storm damage to branches.
seasonal_care.october: Peak acorn drop. Prime food source for wildlife.
seasonal_care.november: Acorn drop continues. Best planting month for new oaks.

common_problems.symptoms: Round or irregular growths on leaves or twigs — can look alarming
common_problems.solution: Caused by tiny wasps — completely harmless to the tree. No treatment needed or recommended. The galls are a food source for some wildlife.

common_problems.symptoms: Individual branches dying back suddenly, especially after storm damage
common_problems.solution: Remove dead branches promptly to prevent pest entry. Paint cut surfaces with wound dressing. If multiple branches affected, contact a certified arborist — may indicate bacterial infection.

common_problems.problem: Resurrection fern browning in dry weather
common_problems.symptoms: Fern on bark turns brown and appears dead
common_problems.solution: Not a problem — this is normal behavior for resurrection fern. It will return to vivid green within hours of rainfall.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at most SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers. Buy the smallest container size available for best transplant success.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at most nurseries throughout Lee and Collier counties
plants.expert_tips: The most important thing to know about live oak is that the root system spreads 2-3x the canopy width underground. Plant it once, plant it right, and give it room. A live oak planted in the wrong spot is a problem that compounds for decades. When in doubt, plant it further from the house than you think you need to.
plants.fun_fact: A single mature live oak can support over 500 species of caterpillars and moths — more than almost any other tree in the Eastern United States. Those caterpillars are the primary food source for nesting songbirds.
plants.traditional_uses: Acorns were a staple food for the Calusa people of SW Florida. The dense hardwood was prized for shipbuilding — USS Constitution ('Old Ironsides') was built largely from live oak timber.
plants.conservation_notes: Live oak hammocks are a critically threatened habitat in SW Florida due to development. Each mature live oak supports a unique ecosystem. Lee and Collier counties protect mature specimens — check local ordinances before any work near a large live oak.

plants.description: Iconic tourist tree with striking peeling red-copper bark. One of SW Florida's fastest growing native trees and exceptionally hurricane resistant. Small fruits eaten by many birds. Extremely drought and salt tolerant. Great for quick canopy cover.
plants.propagation_seed: Seeds viable but rarely used — germination is slow and inconsistent. Cuttings are far easier and faster.
plants.propagation_cutting: Extremely easy from large cuttings — this is the standard method. Cut branches 4–6 feet long, let the cut end dry in shade for 1–2 weeks, then stick directly in the ground or a large pot with sandy soil. Water once to settle soil, then leave alone. Success rate is very high.
plants.germination_method: Surface sow fresh seeds in sandy mix, barely cover.
plants.germination_notes: Seeds lose viability quickly — plant within weeks of collection. Germination is erratic. Stick with cuttings for reliable results.
plants.transplant_notes: One of the easiest trees to transplant in SW Florida. Plant in full sun, well-drained soil. Stakes unnecessary — the flexible trunk benefits from wind movement to develop a strong root system. Water weekly for first 3 months, then leave alone.
plants.looks_like_notes: Poisonwood also has peeling bark and similar leaf shape but has BLACK sap streaks on the bark — extremely toxic, causes severe rash worse than poison ivy. Gumbo limbo has clean copper-red bark with NO black streaks. Always check for black sap before touching any peeling-bark tree in South Florida.
plants.attracts_specific: Red-bellied woodpecker, White-crowned pigeon, Gray catbird, American robin (migration), Cedar waxwing (fruit), Painted bunting (migration stopover)

seasonal_care.january: Dry season — no irrigation needed for established trees. Good month to assess structure and do any light pruning if needed.
seasonal_care.february: Watch for any cold damage on younger trees if temps drop below 30°F. Established trees are fine. No watering needed.
seasonal_care.march: Spring flush of new leaves begins. Small inconspicuous flowers appear. No action needed.
seasonal_care.april: Full leaf out. Hot and dry — newly planted trees need weekly deep watering. Established trees need nothing.
seasonal_care.may: End of dry season. Water new plantings deeply. Watch for any aphid activity on new growth.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season begins — stop supplemental irrigation entirely. Small red fruits begin forming.
seasonal_care.july: Peak rainy season. Tree thrives. Fruits ripening, heavy bird activity. No action needed.
seasonal_care.august: Peak fruit production — watch for migrating birds feeding heavily. Hurricane season peak — gumbo limbo is exceptionally wind-resistant.
seasonal_care.september: Fruits fully ripe, drop naturally. Collect cuttings for propagation this month if desired.
seasonal_care.october: Transition to dry season. Reduce irrigation for newly planted trees. Bird activity continues.
seasonal_care.november: Best month to plant new gumbo limbo. Cooler temps reduce transplant stress.
seasonal_care.december: Fully dormant in terms of active growth. No action needed. Bark peeling is normal and beautiful — do not pick at it.

common_problems.symptoms: Tree loses most or all leaves December–February
common_problems.solution: Normal behavior — gumbo limbo is briefly deciduous in SW Florida winters. New leaves emerge in March. No action needed.

common_problems.symptoms: Reddish-copper outer bark continuously peeling and flaking
common_problems.solution: This is the tree's signature characteristic, not a disease. The peeling bark gives it the nickname 'tourist tree.' Do not treat.

common_problems.problem: Root rot in poorly drained soil
common_problems.symptoms: Yellowing leaves, branch dieback, soft bark at base
common_problems.solution: Gumbo limbo requires well-drained soil — it does not tolerate standing water. Plant in raised areas or improve drainage.

common_problems.symptoms: Brown crusty bumps on branches, sticky honeydew, sooty mold
common_problems.solution: Treat with horticultural oil spray in cooler months. Healthy established trees rarely have serious infestations.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Widely available at SW Florida nurseries. Native plant sales through FNPS Lee/Collier chapters often have smaller sizes at lower prices. Buy the smallest available size — gumbo limbo grows fast and smaller transplants establish better.
plants.expert_tips: You can literally plant a branch. Snap a 4–6 foot limb, let the cut end callous for a week in the shade, stick it in the ground, water once, and walk away. It will root. The peeling bark is also natural sunscreen — the tree reflects excess heat, which is why it thrives in full blazing SW Florida sun with zero care once established.
plants.fun_fact: Gumbo limbo resin was historically used as a treatment for gout and burned as incense. The resin is chemically similar to copal, used in religious ceremonies across Mesoamerica — the tree's range extends to Mexico and the Caribbean.
plants.traditional_uses: The Calusa and Seminole used the resin as a wound salve and insect repellent. The soft lightweight wood was used for fishing floats and carousel horses in the early 20th century due to its easy carving properties.
plants.conservation_notes: Secure native. Common in coastal hammocks throughout SW Florida. Excellent choice for habitat restoration — fast-growing, salt-tolerant, and highly productive for wildlife. Not threatened.

plants.description: Native pine critical to Florida's flatwood ecosystem. Seeds eaten by doves, quail, squirrels, and many songbirds. Host tree for numerous moth and butterfly larvae. Essential cavity nesting sites for woodpeckers, owls, and flying squirrels. Perfectly suited to Cape Coral's well-drained sandy substrate.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect cones when they begin to open in fall. Dry cones in a paper bag until they open fully and release seeds. Sow seeds in sandy acidic mix, barely cover. Keep moist until germination.
plants.propagation_cutting: Not practical — pines do not root from cuttings.
plants.germination_method: Direct sow in sandy acidic mix or direct outdoor sowing.
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seeds germinate readily. No stratification required in SW Florida. Use acidic sandy mix — slash pine dislikes alkaline soils. Seedlings are very delicate for first 6 months.
plants.transplant_notes: Transplant only young container-grown trees — slash pine does not tolerate bare-root transplanting due to mycorrhizal root system. Plant in full sun, well-drained sandy soil only. Avoid clay or alkaline fill soils common in some Cape Coral lots. Do not plant in lawn areas with irrigation — overwatering is the #1 killer of slash pine in residential settings.
plants.looks_like_plants: Longleaf pine (Pinus palustris), Loblolly pine (Pinus taeda)
plants.looks_like_notes: Slash pine has needles in bundles of 2–3 (usually 3), 8–12 inches long, and large cones 3–6 inches. Longleaf pine has much longer needles 10–15 inches and massive cones. For SW Florida, if you see a native pine it is almost certainly slash pine.
plants.attracts_specific: Bachman's sparrow (flatwood specialist), Pileated woodpecker, Hairy woodpecker, Red-bellied woodpecker, Eastern screech owl (cavity nesting), Sherman's fox squirrel, Mourning dove (seeds), Pine warbler

seasonal_care.january: Dry season — no irrigation needed for established trees. Good time to inspect for pine bark beetles if any branches look stressed.
seasonal_care.february: Pollen cones release pollen — heavy yellow pollen is normal and temporary. No action needed.
seasonal_care.march: New growth candles emerge. Do not prune candles. Light fertilization acceptable if tree looks pale.
seasonal_care.april: Active growth. Monitor for pine tip moth on new candles — look for browning tips.
seasonal_care.may: End of dry season. Newly planted trees need deep watering 2x per week. Watch for Ips beetles on stressed trees.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — stop all irrigation. Green cones visible on upper branches.
seasonal_care.july: Fast growth during rainy season. Cones enlarging. No action needed.
seasonal_care.august: Hurricane month — slash pine has excellent wind resistance but monitor large specimens for any leaning.
seasonal_care.september: Cones maturing. Heavy wildlife activity — squirrels, doves, and woodpeckers feeding.
seasonal_care.october: Cones opening and dropping seeds. Best month to plant new slash pines.
seasonal_care.november: Excellent planting month. Cooler temps and reliable moisture help establishment.
seasonal_care.december: Dormant growth period. Needles may look slightly dull — normal. No action needed.

common_problems.symptoms: Reddish-brown boring dust at bark, pitch tubes, rapid crown browning and death
common_problems.solution: Beetles attack stressed or drought-weakened trees. No effective treatment once established — prevention through proper watering and avoiding wounds is key. Remove and chip infested trees promptly to prevent spread.

common_problems.symptoms: Swollen galls on trunk or branches, orange powdery spores in spring
common_problems.solution: Common fungal disease in young slash pines. Minor branch infections can be pruned out. Trunk infections in young trees can be fatal. No chemical treatment recommended for established trees.

common_problems.symptoms: Yellowing needles, crown thinning, death of lower branches first
common_problems.solution: Slash pine dies from too much water faster than from drought. Do not plant in irrigated lawn areas. Ensure excellent drainage. This is the most common cause of slash pine death in residential landscapes.

common_problems.symptoms: Brown dead tips on new spring growth candles
common_problems.solution: Cosmetic damage only on established trees. On young trees, treat with spinosad spray targeting new candle growth in spring.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries and FNPS chapter sales. Less common at big-box stores. Try Aloha Native Plants (Fort Myers) or Koreshan Native Plant Nursery. Buy small — 3-gallon containers establish better than larger specimens.
plants.expert_tips: Slash pine is extremely sensitive to the fill soil that blankets most SW Florida residential lots. If your lot was graded with marl or fill, slash pine will struggle or die within a few years. Dig down before planting — if you hit rock-hard white or gray marl within 18 inches, plant something else. Never top a slash pine — it destroys structure, invites disease, and the tree never recovers.
plants.fun_fact: Slash pine is the dominant tree of the Florida flatwoods ecosystem, which once covered over half of Florida. The trees are fire-adapted — their thick bark protects them from the low-intensity ground fires that historically swept through flatwoods every 3–7 years.
plants.traditional_uses: The Seminole used slash pine resin to waterproof canoes and baskets. Pine needles were used for basket weaving. The turpentine industry heavily harvested slash pine sap throughout Florida from the 1800s through the mid-1900s.
plants.conservation_notes: Florida flatwood ecosystems are critically threatened — over 70% have been lost to development and fire suppression. Each slash pine in a residential landscape provides disproportionate ecological value as remnant flatwood habitat. UF/IFAS strongly supports planting slash pine in appropriate SW Florida locations.

plants.description: Majestic native for wet areas, canal edges, and pond margins. Seeds eaten by wood ducks, sandhill cranes, and many birds. Important nesting habitat for ospreys, herons, and owls. Cypress knees create unique microhabitat. Stunning russet-orange fall color. Extremely long-lived.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect floating cones from water in fall. Dry briefly, extract seeds, cold-stratify for 30–60 days in moist peat in refrigerator, then sow in wet sandy mix. Keep waterlogged — bald cypress seeds need saturated conditions to germinate.
plants.propagation_cutting: Possible but difficult. Take softwood cuttings in early summer, treat with rooting hormone, keep in very humid conditions. Seeds or container nursery stock are more reliable.
plants.germination_method: Cold stratification required, then sow in saturated mix.
plants.germination_notes: Seeds must be kept wet throughout germination. Stratify 30–60 days at 40°F in moist peat, then move to warm saturated conditions.
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants well from container stock. Can be planted in standing water up to 12 inches deep or in normal well-drained soil — bald cypress is remarkably adaptable. Plant at canal edges with the root flare at or slightly above water level. Water deeply every other day for first month if not planted near water.
plants.looks_like_notes: Pond cypress is very similar and also native to SW Florida. Bald cypress has spreading flat needles on horizontal branchlets; pond cypress has appressed needles giving a more rope-like appearance. Both are excellent natives.
plants.attracts_specific: Wood duck (primary cavity nester), Osprey (large branch nesting), Great blue heron (rookery nesting), Anhinga, Barred owl, Prothonotary warbler (cavity nesting), Sandhill crane (foraging near knees), River otter (shelter)

seasonal_care.january: Tree is leafless — this is normal, bald cypress is deciduous. No action needed. Enjoy the interesting silhouette.
seasonal_care.february: Still bare. Root zone is resting. Do not mistake dormancy for death.
seasonal_care.march: New feathery bright green foliage emerges — one of the most beautiful spring events in SW Florida. No action needed.
seasonal_care.april: Full foliage. Small inconspicuous flowers appear. Great time to plant new cypress near water features.
seasonal_care.may: Active growth. Water deeply weekly for newly planted trees through the end of dry season.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — tree thrives with increased water availability. Small round green cones visible.
seasonal_care.july: Peak growth period. Trees in or near water grow fastest. Cones enlarging.
seasonal_care.august: Cones maturing to purple-brown. Hurricane winds rarely damage well-rooted bald cypress.
seasonal_care.september: Foliage beginning to show russet tones — early color change. Cones dropping.
seasonal_care.october: Peak fall color — russet to brick-orange, one of the best fall color displays in SW Florida.
seasonal_care.november: Needles dropping. Collect seed cones from water surface for propagation.
seasonal_care.december: Fully leafless. Cypress knees visible. No action needed.

common_problems.symptoms: Brown dead twig tips, small black fruiting bodies on dead tissue
common_problems.solution: Prune affected tips. Improve drainage if in poorly drained upland site. Rarely fatal.

common_problems.symptoms: Grayish aphids on stems, sticky honeydew, sooty mold, branch dieback
common_problems.solution: Treat with strong water spray or insecticidal soap. Avoid broad-spectrum pesticides near water.

common_problems.symptoms: Yellowing needles with green veins, poor growth
common_problems.solution: Apply sulfur to acidify or use chelated iron. Trees planted at water's edge rarely show this problem.

common_problems.symptoms: All needles turn brown and fall off in winter
common_problems.solution: Completely normal — bald cypress is deciduous. The 'bald' in the name refers to this winter leaf drop. New growth emerges bright green in March.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native nurseries across SW Florida. Excellent availability at SFWMD and SWFMD native plant giveaway events — check their websites for free or subsidized native tree programs. Also available at Aloha Native Plants and many Lowe's/Home Depot garden centers in season.
plants.expert_tips: The cypress knees are pneumatophores that help the tree breathe in waterlogged soil — do not remove or damage them. Bald cypress is far more drought-tolerant than people assume. You can successfully grow it in normal well-drained residential soil with regular watering. The fall color (October–November) is the best autumn display available to SW Florida gardeners.
plants.fun_fact: Bald cypress wood is extraordinarily rot-resistant — sometimes called 'wood eternal.' Ancient buried cypress logs in Florida swamps have been recovered after thousands of years and are still structurally sound enough to mill into lumber.
plants.traditional_uses: The Seminole used hollowed cypress logs as dugout canoes, water storage vessels, and mortars for grinding corn. The rot-resistant wood was the primary building material for Florida's early settler structures, fish camps, and docks.
plants.conservation_notes: Bald cypress strands and domes are a critically threatened Florida ecosystem. Most old-growth cypress was logged in the early 1900s. Planting bald cypress along canals and water features directly supports habitat restoration. Lee and Collier counties encourage cypress planting along waterways.

plants.description: Native holly producing masses of bright red berries that cedar waxwings, robins, and mockingbirds devour in winter. Tolerates wet areas well. Can be grown as a large shrub or small tree. Female plants need a nearby male for berry production.
warnings: Berries are toxic to humans and pets — do not ingest.
plants.growth_notes: Moderate growth, faster in moist sites
plants.pruning_notes: Minimal pruning needed. Shape lightly in spring.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Tolerates wet areas, drought, and salt. Very adaptable.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, winter berry food source for birds, nesting habitat
plants.propagation_seed: Collect berries when ripe red. Clean pulp. Cold stratify 60-90 days before sowing.
plants.germination_method: Cold stratify then sow in moist mix
plants.germination_notes: Cold stratification greatly improves germination
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants well from container. Tolerates wet planting sites. Plant male and female for berries.
plants.looks_like_notes: Dahoon holly identified by clusters of bright red berries, narrow lance-shaped leaves, and tolerance of wet sites. Inkberry (I. glabra) has black berries and is also native.
plants.attracts_specific: Cedar waxwing (primary winter berry consumer), American robin, Hermit thrush, Gray catbird

common_problems.symptoms: Flowers but no berry production
common_problems.solution: Dahoon holly is dioecious — separate male and female plants required. Ensure at least one male plant within 50 ft of female plants. Wind and bees transfer pollen.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries throughout SW Florida.
plants.expert_tips: Plant male and female together for berry production — this is the most commonly overlooked requirement. One male will pollinate several females within range.
plants.fun_fact: Cedar waxwings eat the berries so quickly that the display can last only days when a flock arrives. Plant multiple specimens to extend the food supply.
plants.traditional_uses: Berries used in folk medicine by various cultures for their emetic properties. Not recommended for consumption.
plants.conservation_notes: Dahoon holly is one of the most important winter food plants for migrating birds in SW Florida. Populations have declined with the loss of wetland habitats.

plants.description: One of the most bird-attractive fruiting trees in Florida. Rose-breasted grosbeaks, scarlet tanagers, catbirds, and dozens of other species flock to it during fruiting in spring. Berries also eaten by raccoons, opossums, and foxes. Edible for humans — sweet and abundant.
plants.growth_notes: Fast growing fruit tree
plants.pruning_notes: Prune after fruiting season to control size. Annual pruning encourages new fruiting wood.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Very easy in SW Florida. Tolerates range of conditions.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, major spring bird food source, mammals, dual food garden and wildlife value
plants.propagation_seed: Seeds germinate readily but fruiting quality variable. Buy named varieties for best fruit.
plants.propagation_cutting: Softwood cuttings in spring. Moderately difficult.
plants.germination_method: Sow fresh cleaned seed in well-drained mix
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seed germinates better than stored.
plants.transplant_notes: Container plants transplant well. Provide plenty of space — trees spread wide. Berry drop will stain pavement.
do_not_plant_near: Paved areas, driveways, light-colored surfaces — falling berries cause significant staining
plants.looks_like_notes: White mulberry was introduced and has naturalized in some areas. Red mulberry has slightly larger leaves with a rough upper surface. White mulberry leaves are smoother and glossier.
plants.attracts_specific: Rose-breasted grosbeak (major consumer), Scarlet tanager, Gray catbird, Northern mockingbird, American robin, Cedar waxwing, Raccoon, Opossum, Fox squirrel

common_problems.symptoms: Purple-red stains on surfaces below tree
common_problems.solution: Plant away from any paved areas or light-colored surfaces. The staining is difficult to remove. Plan placement carefully — the berries are a feature, not a bug.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries. Red mulberry is less commonly available than the non-native white mulberry — verify species.
plants.expert_tips: Red mulberry has one of the most concentrated wildlife feeding events of any SW Florida tree. When it fruits in spring, the sheer number and variety of bird species visiting can be extraordinary — it's worth planting in a visible spot from your home for the spring bird watching alone.
plants.fun_fact: Red mulberry is the host plant for the silkworm moth — though the commercial silk industry uses white mulberry. Red mulberry silk was used by some Native American peoples.
plants.traditional_uses: Berries eaten fresh and used for jams, jellies, pies, and wine by Native American peoples and European settlers. The wood was used for fence posts and furniture.
plants.conservation_notes: Red mulberry populations have declined in the Southeast due to displacement by the invasive white mulberry and hybridization between the two species. Planting true red mulberry supports the native species.

plants.description: Fast-growing native that works as a large shrub or small multi-trunk tree. Waxy gray berries are the primary winter food source for yellow-rumped warblers and many other migrating birds. Nitrogen-fixer that improves soil health. Highly salt tolerant and adaptable.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect ripe blue-gray berries, remove waxy coating by rubbing in sand, sow in sandy mix. Cold stratification (30 days at 40°F) improves germination rates but is not strictly required in SW Florida.
plants.propagation_cutting: Easy from semi-hardwood cuttings taken in summer. Take 4–6 inch cuttings, strip lower leaves, dip in rooting hormone, plant in moist sandy perlite mix, keep humid. Roots in 4–6 weeks.
plants.propagation_division: Clumping multi-stem plants can be divided by digging and separating root suckers from the base.
plants.germination_method: Sow in sandy mix after removing waxy coating. Cold stratification optional.
plants.germination_notes: Wax coating inhibits germination — must be removed before sowing. Germination is erratic without stratification. Cuttings are much faster and easier.
plants.transplant_notes: Extremely adaptable — transplants easily at most sizes. Plant in full sun to partial shade in nearly any well-drained soil. Space 6–10 feet apart for hedge use, or allow to develop naturally as a multi-trunk small tree 15–20 feet tall. Water weekly for first 3 months, then drought-tolerant.
plants.looks_like_notes: Young wax myrtle can resemble Brazilian pepper. Key difference: wax myrtle leaves are olive-green, aromatic when crushed (bayberry scent). Brazilian pepper leaves smell like turpentine/pepper when crushed and have a distinctive winged central leaf stem.
plants.attracts_specific: Yellow-rumped warbler (primary winter food), Tree swallow (berries during migration), Eastern bluebird, Northern mockingbird, Gray catbird, Carolina wren (nesting), Ruby-throated hummingbird (flowers), Honeybee

seasonal_care.january: Peak berry season — waxy gray berries are primary food for yellow-rumped warblers and migrating birds. Do not prune now.
seasonal_care.february: Berry crop continues. No action needed. Birds heavily dependent on this food source through end of winter.
seasonal_care.march: Berry crop winding down. Best month to do any shaping or pruning if needed — before new growth flush.
seasonal_care.april: New growth flush. Inconspicuous flowers appear. Light fertilization optional.
seasonal_care.may: Rapid growth — one of SW Florida's fastest native shrub-trees. End of dry season — water new plantings deeply.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — stop irrigation. Very fast growth. Can be lightly shaped if getting too large.
seasonal_care.july: Peak growth. New berry clusters forming on female plants.
seasonal_care.august: Green berries visible. Hurricane-resistant due to flexible multi-stem structure.
seasonal_care.september: Berries ripening to blue-gray. Good month to plant new wax myrtles.
seasonal_care.october: Berries nearly ripe. Migrating birds begin arriving — yellow-rumped warblers appear.
seasonal_care.november: Berry season peaks with arrival of winter migrants. Best planting month.
seasonal_care.december: Full berry production. Do not prune. Bird activity at its peak.

common_problems.symptoms: Pale yellow-green leaves, slow growth
common_problems.solution: Wax myrtle is a nitrogen fixer and rarely needs fertilizer. If yellowing persists, apply a slow-release fertilizer with iron and micronutrients. Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers.

common_problems.symptoms: Brown crusty bumps on stems, sticky honeydew, sooty mold, branch dieback
common_problems.solution: Treat with horticultural oil in cooler months (November–March). Healthy plants rarely have serious issues.

common_problems.symptoms: Plant reduced to stubs, loses natural form, excessive weak regrowth
common_problems.solution: Wax myrtle's wildlife value is in its natural multi-stem billowing form. Thin selectively rather than shearing.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: One of the most widely available Florida natives. Found at most SW Florida nurseries, big-box garden centers, and all native plant sales. Very inexpensive in small sizes. Buy several — it looks best in groupings.
plants.expert_tips: Wax myrtle is dioecious — you need both male and female plants to get berries. When buying at a nursery, ask for female plants or buy a mix. This tree fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root bacteria, actively improving the soil around it — great planted near heavy feeders like palms.
plants.fun_fact: The yellow-rumped warbler depends so heavily on wax myrtle berries that it's sometimes called the 'myrtle warbler.' It's one of the few warblers that can digest the waxy coating on the berries — a specialized digestive adaptation that gives it access to a food source other birds can't fully utilize.
plants.traditional_uses: Waxy berries were boiled to extract bayberry wax for candle-making. The aromatic leaves were used by Seminole as an insect repellent and in medicinal teas for fever and cold symptoms. Roots and bark used for stomach ailments.
plants.conservation_notes: Common and secure native. Found in coastal scrub, flatwoods edges, and disturbed areas throughout SW Florida. One of the most wildlife-valuable plants per square foot of any native. Highly recommended by UF/IFAS and FNPS for habitat restoration.

plants.description: Native fruiting tree whose sweet fall fruits feed bluebirds, mockingbirds, warblers, raccoons, foxes, and deer. Edible for humans after fruits fully ripen — unripe fruits are very astringent. Host tree for luna moth and royal walnut moth caterpillars.
warnings: Unripe fruits are extremely astringent — wait until fully soft and ripe before eating.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect seeds from fully ripe soft fruits. Clean pulp off seeds, cold-stratify 60–90 days in moist peat at 40°F, then sow 1 inch deep in sandy mix. Note: persimmon is dioecious — seedlings will be a mix of male and female.
plants.propagation_cutting: Difficult — not recommended for home propagation. Root cuttings taken in late winter have moderate success with rooting hormone.
plants.propagation_division: Root suckers can be dug and transplanted. Persimmon produces suckers around the base that are already rooted.
plants.germination_method: Cold stratification 60–90 days, then sow 1 inch deep in sandy mix.
plants.germination_notes: Stratification is important — seeds germinate poorly without a cold period. Outdoor sowing in December–January in SW Florida often works as natural stratification.
plants.transplant_notes: Transplant young container-grown trees only — persimmon has a deep taproot that does not transplant well bare-root. Plant in full sun to partial shade. Water weekly for full first year. Persimmon is slow to establish but very long-lived.
plants.looks_like_plants: Water tupelo (Nyssa aquatica), Black gum (Nyssa sylvatica)
plants.looks_like_notes: Persimmon is most distinctive when fruiting. Vegetatively, the deeply checkered dark bark in a rectangular block pattern is unique and diagnostic. Tupelo species have smoother bark and different leaf shape.
plants.attracts_specific: Eastern bluebird, American robin, Northern mockingbird, Gray catbird, Cedar waxwing, White-eyed vireo, Luna moth (host plant), Royal walnut moth (host plant), Raccoon, Virginia opossum, White-tailed deer, Gray fox

seasonal_care.january: Any remaining fruits on tree are fully ripe and intensely sweet after cold nights. Excellent wildlife feeding time. No action needed.
seasonal_care.february: Tree may be semi-deciduous in cooler winters. Some leaf drop is normal. No action needed.
seasonal_care.march: New leaf flush. Good time for light pruning to shape canopy if needed.
seasonal_care.april: Full foliage. Small inconspicuous creamy flowers appear on female trees.
seasonal_care.may: Flowers pollinated, tiny green fruits forming. End of dry season — water new plantings.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season begins — stop irrigation. Fruits enlarging slowly through summer.
seasonal_care.july: Green fruits visible, still hard and very astringent. Do not eat yet.
seasonal_care.august: Fruits enlarging. Tree looks healthy and full.
seasonal_care.september: Fruits beginning to color — yellow-orange. Still astringent — wait for full ripeness.
seasonal_care.october: Fruits ripening. Wait until soft and fully orange before eating. Wildlife beginning to feed.
seasonal_care.november: Peak fruit drop. Best wildlife activity. Collect ripe fallen fruits for seed propagation.
seasonal_care.december: Late fruits persist. Best planting month for new persimmons. Any frost sweetens remaining fruits.

common_problems.symptoms: Tree flowers but produces no fruit, or never flowers
common_problems.solution: American persimmon is dioecious — you need both a male and female tree nearby to get fruit. Plant at least two trees. Grafted named varieties are self-fertile alternatives.

common_problems.symptoms: Curled or puckered new leaves, tiny jumping insects visible
common_problems.solution: Usually minor — healthy trees outgrow the damage. Treat with insecticidal soap if severe on young trees.

common_problems.symptoms: Hard green or yellow fruits dropping in summer
common_problems.solution: Normal — persimmon naturally thins its fruit crop. Only harvest fruits that have softened completely and fallen naturally.

common_problems.symptoms: Brown or black spots on leaves, premature leaf drop
common_problems.solution: Usually not serious in SW Florida. Improve air circulation by thinning canopy. Rarely requires treatment.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Less common at big-box stores — look at native plant nurseries and FNPS sales. Some specialty fruit tree nurseries carry grafted named varieties (Meader, Prok) which are self-fertile and more reliable for fruit production than seedlings.
plants.expert_tips: The astringency of unripe persimmons is no joke — one bite will leave your mouth feeling like it's coated in chalk for an hour. Wait until the fruit is almost embarrassingly soft and wrinkled, ideally after a cold snap. In SW Florida where hard freezes are rare, leave fruit on the tree until it drops naturally. The gnarly dark-checkered bark makes it architecturally interesting year-round.
plants.fun_fact: American persimmon wood is the same genus as ebony and is one of the hardest woods in North America. It was historically used to make golf club heads and textile shuttles. The scientific name Diospyros means 'fruit of the gods' in Greek.
plants.traditional_uses: A critical food source for the Calusa and Seminole. Fruits were eaten fresh, dried for winter storage, or fermented. Seeds were roasted as a coffee substitute during the Civil War. Bark tea was used medicinally for fevers and sore throats.
plants.conservation_notes: Secure native, common in upland habitats throughout Florida. The tree's wildlife value is exceptional — over 40 species of birds and mammals eat the fruit in Florida. An underused landscape tree that deserves far more planting.

plants.description: Evergreen native with blue-gray berries eaten by many birds — cedar waxwings are literally named for this tree. Dense fragrant foliage provides year-round nesting cover. Very salt and drought tolerant. Often protected under county tree ordinances.
warnings: Often protected by county ordinances — check local regulations before removing mature specimens.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect ripe blue berries, remove fleshy coating, cold-stratify seeds 30–60 days, then sow in sandy well-drained mix. Germination is slow and erratic.
plants.propagation_cutting: Semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer/fall with rooting hormone. Wound the cutting base, dip in IBA rooting hormone, plant in sandy perlite mix, keep humid. Takes 2–3 months to root.
plants.germination_method: Cold stratification 30–60 days, then sow in well-drained sandy mix.
plants.germination_notes: Germination is notoriously slow and irregular in junipers. Cuttings are preferred for faster more reliable results.
plants.transplant_notes: Requires full sun and excellent drainage — will not tolerate wet feet or shade. Sandy soil is ideal. Plant with root flare at or slightly above grade. Do not mulch heavily against the trunk. Water weekly for first 6 months, then leave alone. Check local ordinances — mature specimens are often protected in Lee and Collier counties.
plants.looks_like_notes: Nearly identical to eastern red cedar. Juniperus silicicola has slightly smaller berries and more pendulous branch tips. For landscape purposes they are functionally interchangeable, but silicicola is the correct native choice for SW Florida.
plants.attracts_specific: Cedar waxwing (primary — named for this tree), Yellow-rumped warbler, American robin, Eastern bluebird, Northern mockingbird, Gray catbird, Dark-eyed junco (winter), Carolina wren (dense nesting cover), Eastern red bat (roost)

seasonal_care.january: Blue-gray berries at peak. Heavy bird activity — cedar waxwings, yellow-rumped warblers, robins. Do not prune now.
seasonal_care.february: Berry season continues. One of the best months to plant new cedars — cool weather reduces stress.
seasonal_care.march: Pollen cones release yellow pollen — may be heavy and visible. No action needed. New growth begins.
seasonal_care.april: Active new growth. Best time to do light shaping if needed — before summer heat.
seasonal_care.may: Rapid growth in hot dry weather. New berry clusters forming. Water new plantings.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — stop irrigation. Fast growth continues.
seasonal_care.july: Green berries forming and enlarging. Tree thrives in summer heat.
seasonal_care.august: Berries maturing. Hurricane-resistant due to dense flexible branching.
seasonal_care.september: Berries ripening to blue. Good month to plant new cedars.
seasonal_care.october: Berries fully ripe — blue-gray waxy coating visible. Bird activity picking up.
seasonal_care.november: Berry season peaks with arrival of winter migrants. Best planting month.
seasonal_care.december: Full berry crop. Cedar waxwing flocks arrive to strip berries. Peak wildlife value.

common_problems.symptoms: Brown dead branch tips, may progress inward along branches
common_problems.solution: Improve air circulation, avoid overhead irrigation. Prune affected tips back to healthy wood. Copper fungicide spray in spring as preventive.

common_problems.symptoms: Small cone-shaped bags of silk and plant material hanging from branches; defoliation if severe
common_problems.solution: Handpick bags in fall and winter when visible. Bt spray in spring when caterpillars are small. Remove bags before they open in spring.

common_problems.problem: Root rot in clay or wet soil
common_problems.symptoms: Browning from base up, soft trunk base, death
common_problems.solution: Southern red cedar requires excellent drainage. Do not plant in low spots or near irrigation heads. No recovery once root rot is established.

common_problems.symptoms: Dusty gray-green foliage, fine webbing, stippled bronzing of foliage
common_problems.solution: Hose off with strong water spray. Miticide spray if severe. More common during prolonged dry spells.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries — ask specifically for Juniperus silicicola to ensure you get the SW Florida native species. FNPS chapter sales are the most reliable source for correctly identified native stock.
plants.expert_tips: Southern red cedar and eastern red cedar (Juniperus virginiana) are often sold interchangeably at nurseries, but silicicola is the true SW Florida native. The blue 'berries' are technically seed cones. The aromatic wood is naturally moth-repellent. If you have a large specimen, check with Lee or Collier county before significant pruning — mature trees are often protected under canopy ordinances.
plants.fun_fact: Cedar waxwings are literally named after this tree — their preferred food and the waxy red tips on their wing feathers gave them both parts of their name. A single southern red cedar can host hundreds of waxwings at once during winter, stripping every berry in a matter of hours.
plants.traditional_uses: Aromatic wood used for storage chests and closet linings to repel moths and insects. Seminole used the fragrant wood in ceremonial fires. Berries used medicinally for respiratory ailments. The dense evergreen canopy was used as natural windbreaks and privacy screening.
plants.conservation_notes: Common native throughout SW Florida coastal areas and well-drained uplands. Provides critical year-round cover for nesting birds. Protected under mature tree ordinances in many municipalities.

plants.description: One of the most wildlife-productive trees in Florida — fruit eaten by 28+ bird species. Supports enormous insect diversity. Begins life as an epiphyte before becoming a freestanding tree. Protected tree in many FL counties.
warnings: Roots are very aggressive near hardscape and foundations. Plant well away from structures. Protected tree in many counties — check before removing.
plants.propagation_seed: Tiny seeds found inside the figs. Rarely practical — figs require specific fig wasp pollinators for seed set. Extract seeds from ripe figs, sow on surface of moist mix, do not cover.
plants.propagation_cutting: Very easy from large cuttings. Take 12–24 inch hardwood cuttings, allow cut end to dry 24–48 hours to let milky sap seal, then stick in moist sandy soil. Roots readily in warm months.
plants.propagation_division: Not applicable for trees. Air layering works well on branches — girdle a branch, wrap with moist sphagnum moss, cover with plastic, wait 6–8 weeks for roots.
plants.germination_method: Surface sow on moist mix, no covering.
plants.germination_notes: Seed propagation is rarely practical without native fig wasp. Cuttings or air layers are the standard approach.
plants.transplant_notes: Plant ONLY in locations far from foundations, pools, driveways, and utility lines — minimum 30 feet from any structure. The root system is extraordinarily aggressive. Container trees transplant easily. Water weekly for first year.
plants.looks_like_plants: Shortleaf fig (Ficus citrifolia), Clusia (Clusia rosea, C. guttifera)
plants.looks_like_notes: Shortleaf fig (Ficus citrifolia) is also native to SW Florida and very similar — it has slightly smaller leaves and less aggressive roots. Clusia has similar thick shiny leaves but Clusia leaves are thick and paddle-shaped; fig leaves are thinner. The milky sap when breaking a leaf or twig is diagnostic for all figs.
plants.attracts_specific: Red-bellied woodpecker, Pileated woodpecker, White-crowned pigeon, Gray catbird, Northern mockingbird, Cedar waxwing, Swainson's thrush (migration), Short-tailed hawk (hunting), Raccoon, Gray squirrel

seasonal_care.january: Dry season. Established trees need no irrigation. Good month to observe structure — birds most visible foraging in the canopy.
seasonal_care.february: Tree may produce a flush of small figs. Migratory birds feeding heavily on fruit. No action needed.
seasonal_care.march: New leaf flush on some trees. No action needed. If planted near structures, inspect roots.
seasonal_care.april: Active growth. Fig production cycle underway. No action needed.
seasonal_care.may: End of dry season. Young planted trees need deep watering.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — stop irrigation. Fast growth. Heavy fruit production begins.
seasonal_care.july: Peak fruiting for many trees — massive wildlife activity. No action needed.
seasonal_care.august: Continued heavy fruit production. Hurricane month — mature figs are very wind-resistant due to deep anchoring root systems.
seasonal_care.september: Fruit production continues. One of the busiest wildlife months around a mature strangler fig.
seasonal_care.october: Fruit may slow. Good month to plant new figs away from structures.
seasonal_care.november: Good planting month. Assess any root encroachment near hardscape and address early.
seasonal_care.december: Dry season begins. Reduce irrigation for new plants. Some leaf drop is normal.

common_problems.symptoms: Cracked driveways, lifted pavers, damaged pool decks, foundation intrusion
common_problems.solution: Prevention only — plant far from all hardscape. There is no effective root barrier for mature figs. If causing damage near a structure, removal may be the only solution. Check county tree protection ordinances before removal.

common_problems.symptoms: Skin irritation, rash on contact with milky sap from broken branches or leaves
common_problems.solution: Wear gloves when pruning. Wash skin immediately with soap and water after sap contact. Avoid eye contact — sap is a serious eye irritant.

common_problems.symptoms: White powder on undersides of leaves, yellowing, premature leaf drop, white coating on upper leaf surface
common_problems.solution: A serious pest of ornamental figs in South Florida. Treat with systemic insecticide (imidacloprid soil drench) in spring before populations build. This pest has devastated many ornamental ficus hedges in SW Florida — monitor closely.

common_problems.symptoms: Aerial roots wrapping around and eventually girdling a host palm or tree
common_problems.solution: This is the tree's natural growth strategy. If you want to prevent it from strangling a host tree, remove the fig while still small. Once mature, the strangling process is part of the tree's ecological role.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries. Best sourced as a young small plant. FNPS chapter sales sometimes have small specimens. Given the root system, buy small and plant in the right spot from day one.
plants.expert_tips: Strangler fig is arguably the single most wildlife-productive tree you can plant in SW Florida — 28+ bird species eat the fruit. But it must be planted in the right place. Think of it as a tree for large naturalistic lots, conservation land, and canal banks — not a suburban backyard. The tree starts life as an epiphyte (a seed dropped into a palm crown) — in your landscape, planted as a ground tree, it skips straight to the terrestrial phase.
plants.fun_fact: The strangler fig's relationship with its specific fig wasp pollinator is one of the most precise co-evolutionary relationships in nature. Each fig species has its own dedicated wasp species. The tiny wasps enter through a barely-visible pore in the fig, pollinate flowers inside, lay eggs, and die inside the fig. You have likely eaten fig wasps — they are digested along with the fruit.
plants.traditional_uses: The Calusa used the broad shade of large strangler figs as gathering places. The latex sap was used as a crude adhesive and waterproofing agent. Aerial roots were used for cordage. Ripe figs were eaten by indigenous peoples.
plants.conservation_notes: Native and ecologically critical. Strangler fig hammocks are a threatened habitat type in SW Florida. The tree is protected under canopy ordinances in Lee, Collier, and Charlotte counties — verify before any significant pruning or removal.

plants.description: Classic coastal native highly tolerant of salt, wind, and drought. A keystone of SW Florida's coastal hammock habitat. Can be maintained as a clipped formal hedge or allowed to grow into an attractive multi-trunk tree.
plants.growth_notes: Moderate to fast growth. Very adaptable.
plants.pruning_notes: Excellent hedge plant. Can be sheared to any size or allowed to grow naturally. Very tolerant of hard pruning.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: One of the most adaptable and tough native plants for SW Florida coastal conditions.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, coastal habitat keystone, caterpillar host, bird seeds and nesting, hurricane tough
plants.propagation_seed: Collect seed heads when brown. Sow in sandy well-drained mix.
plants.germination_notes: Good germination rate in well-drained conditions.
plants.transplant_notes: Extremely easy to transplant. Very forgiving. Tolerates salt spray, wind, poor soil, and drought from day one.
plants.looks_like_notes: The spongy button-like seed heads in clusters are distinctive. The small dark leathery leaves and tolerance of coastal conditions make it recognizable.
plants.attracts_specific: Mangrove cuckoo (nesting), White-crowned pigeon (seeds), Migratory warblers (insects in canopy)

common_problems.problem: Chlorosis in non-coastal high pH soils
common_problems.symptoms: Yellowing leaves despite good water
common_problems.solution: Buttonwood actually prefers alkaline coastal conditions. Chlorosis rare in its preferred coastal habitat. If occurring, verify drainage is adequate.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at most SW Florida native nurseries and coastal landscaping specialists.
plants.expert_tips: Buttonwood is one of very few native plants that bridges upland and mangrove zones. It can be planted right at the edge of mangrove habitat where almost nothing else will grow, and it establishes a transition zone that supports both upland and wetland wildlife.
plants.fun_fact: Buttonwood is considered the landward edge of the mangrove zone — it bridges the gap between terrestrial and marine ecosystems, one of the most biologically productive transition zones on earth.
plants.traditional_uses: The dense hard wood was used for charcoal production and fuel wood historically. The charcoal was considered exceptionally high quality.
plants.conservation_notes: Buttonwood is a key component of SW Florida's coastal hammock habitat, one of the most threatened ecosystems in the region due to sea level rise and development.

plants.description: Iconic coastal native with huge round leathery leaves and grape-like fruit clusters. Fruits are edible for humans — used in jams and jellies — and eaten by many birds and mammals. Extremely salt and drought tolerant.
warnings: Protected by Florida statute near coastlines — trimming may require permits. Check local regulations before pruning.
plants.growth_notes: Moderate growth. Faster in full sun.
plants.pruning_notes: Can be maintained as a hedge or small tree. Hard prune tolerant.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Very easy in coastal SW Florida. Extremely salt and drought tolerant.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, edible fruit for humans and wildlife, coastal habitat value, large ornamental leaves
plants.propagation_seed: Plant fresh berries directly in sandy soil. Remove pulp first.
plants.propagation_cutting: Semi-hardwood cuttings root in warm conditions.
plants.germination_method: Sow fresh cleaned seed in sandy mix
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seed germinates much better than dried.
plants.transplant_notes: Very easy to transplant. Tolerates full coastal exposure immediately after planting. Salt spray does not harm it.
plants.looks_like_notes: Sea grape has the largest and most distinctive leaves of any common coastal tree — huge round leathery leaves with red veins. Pigeon plum has smaller narrower leaves. Sea grape is unmistakable.
plants.attracts_specific: White-crowned pigeon (primary fruit consumer — this pigeon depends heavily on sea grape), Northern mockingbird, Raccoon, White-tailed deer

seasonal_care.april: Flowering — small fragrant white flowers on long racemes

common_problems.symptoms: N/A — regulatory issue not a plant problem
common_problems.solution: Sea grape is protected by Florida statute in coastal areas. Trimming seagrape seaward of the coastal construction control line requires a permit from the Florida DEP. Always check permit requirements before any pruning near the coast.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at most SW Florida nurseries. One of the most popular native coastal plants.
plants.expert_tips: Sea grape jelly is a genuine SW Florida culinary tradition. The grapes are small with large seeds but the jelly has a unique mild fruity flavor worth making. Harvest when the clusters turn deep purple-black — taste one first to check ripeness.
plants.fun_fact: Sea grape leaves have been used as natural plates and writing surfaces — the large leathery leaves can be written on with a stick or nail, earning the plant its folk name 'sea grape paper.'
plants.traditional_uses: Fruit eaten fresh and made into jelly and wine throughout the Caribbean. Bark and leaves used medicinally in traditional Caribbean medicine.
plants.conservation_notes: Sea grape is one of the defining plants of SW Florida's coastal landscape. Its populations are declining due to coastal development and sea level rise, making each cultivated specimen an act of conservation.
plants.hoa_notes: Protected by Florida statute near coastlines — HOAs cannot require removal in protected zones.

plants.description: One of SW Florida's most spectacular small native trees. Clusters of vivid orange trumpet flowers bloom nearly year-round and are a magnet for hummingbirds and bees. Very salt and drought tolerant. Stays relatively small at 15-25 ft — perfect for smaller yards.
plants.growth_notes: Moderate growth. Flowers continuously once established.
plants.pruning_notes: Prune lightly after heavy bloom cycles to maintain size.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: One of the most rewarding small native trees for SW Florida. Drought and salt tolerant.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, year-round hummingbird magnet, bee forage, bird food, small size ideal for residential
plants.propagation_seed: Collect white drupes when soft and ripe. Clean and sow fresh.
plants.propagation_cutting: Semi-hardwood cuttings root in warm conditions.
plants.germination_method: Sow fresh cleaned seed in sandy mix
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seed performs much better than dried.
plants.transplant_notes: Excellent transplant tolerance. Plant in fall for best establishment. Does not need irrigation after first few months.
plants.looks_like_notes: The native Geiger tree has distinctive rough-textured dark green leaves and brilliant orange flowers. Unmistakable when in bloom.
plants.attracts_specific: Ruby-throated hummingbird (primary pollinator), Broad-tailed hummingbird (winter visitor), Honeybees, White-crowned pigeon (fruit)

common_problems.problem: Leaf scorch in full coastal exposure
common_problems.symptoms: Brown leaf edges in salt spray areas
common_problems.solution: Geiger tree is among the most salt tolerant natives but extreme direct spray can cause temporary leaf scorch. Recovery is rapid. No treatment needed.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries throughout SW Florida. Worth seeking out — not always at big box stores.
plants.expert_tips: The Geiger tree is named for John Geiger, a 19th-century Key West pilot and wrecker who had a large specimen growing at his home. It remains an iconic plant of Florida's coastal communities. Plant one near a window where you can see hummingbirds.
plants.fun_fact: The Geiger tree is the unofficial symbol of Key West and appears in John James Audubon's famous painting of the white-crowned pigeon feeding on its fruit during his 1832 visit to Florida.
plants.traditional_uses: The bark has been used medicinally in Caribbean folk medicine for chest complaints and coughs.
plants.conservation_notes: The native Geiger tree is increasingly rare in SW Florida's natural coastal hammocks due to development. Each cultivated specimen preserves the species in the landscape.

plants.description: Florida's native mahogany — a beautiful broad canopy tree of South Florida's tropical hardwood hammocks. Seeds in large woody pods eaten by parrots and other birds. Host plant for several moth species. Semi-deciduous in late winter.
plants.growth_notes: Moderate growth. Long-lived and increasingly beautiful with age.
plants.pruning_notes: Remove dead wood only. Do not top. Shape lightly if needed.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Requires good drainage and full sun. More specific needs than some natives.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, seed food for parrots and birds, host plant, semi-deciduous spectacle
plants.propagation_seed: Collect winged seeds from pods before pods open fully. Sow fresh in sandy mix.
plants.germination_method: Sow fresh winged seeds in well-drained sandy mix
plants.germination_notes: Germination typically good when fresh. Seeds lose viability quickly.
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants reasonably well when young. Very difficult as a large specimen. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage.
do_not_plant_near: Low wet areas — does not tolerate waterlogged conditions
plants.looks_like_notes: Florida native mahogany is distinguished by its smaller leaves and seed pods compared to the Central American species. The peeling gray bark and semi-deciduous habit in late winter are identifying features.
plants.attracts_specific: Cuban amazon parrot (seeds — historically), Red-bellied woodpecker (insects in bark), Various moth species (host plant)

common_problems.problem: Poor growth in wet or alkaline soils
common_problems.symptoms: Yellowing, poor growth, dieback
common_problems.solution: Florida mahogany requires excellent drainage and performs best in slightly acidic sandy soil. Alkaline muck or clay soils significantly reduce performance. Plant in native sandy substrate.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries. Less commonly available than many other natives.
plants.expert_tips: Florida mahogany is essentially the only native tree in North America producing the famous fine-grained furniture wood. Old-growth specimens were logged to near extinction — planting one is a genuine conservation act and a multi-generational gift.
plants.fun_fact: USS Constitution, the world's oldest commissioned naval vessel still afloat, was built largely from live oak and Florida mahogany. The wood's strength and beauty made it the most valuable timber in the New World.
plants.traditional_uses: The wood has been one of the most prized furniture woods in the world for centuries. Seminole people used the wood for tools and implements.
plants.conservation_notes: Florida native mahogany is listed as endangered in the wild in South Florida due to historical logging and current development. The Big Cypress and Everglades areas hold the remaining natural populations.

plants.description: Small native tree with intensely fragrant golden-yellow puffball flowers in late winter and spring when little else is blooming — a critical early nectar source for bees and butterflies. Very drought tolerant. Thorny habit provides excellent protected nesting cover.
warnings: Has sharp thorns — plant away from high foot traffic areas.
plants.growth_notes: Fast growing small tree
plants.pruning_notes: Remove dead wood. Light shaping acceptable. Avoid pruning when bees actively foraging on flowers.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Very easy and drought tolerant. The thorns require thoughtful siting.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, critical early spring bee food, butterfly forage, protective nesting cover from thorns
plants.propagation_seed: Collect seed pods when dry. Scarify seeds or soak in hot water 24hr before sowing.
plants.propagation_cutting: Not commonly done. Seed is easier.
plants.germination_method: Sow scarified seed in sandy well-drained mix
plants.germination_notes: Hard seed coat requires scarification for reliable germination.
plants.transplant_notes: Easy to transplant when young. Site away from foot traffic areas due to thorns. Excellent for property boundaries.
do_not_plant_near: Walkways, play areas, pet areas — the thorns are very sharp
plants.looks_like_notes: Sweet acacia identified by its small bipinnate leaves, intensely fragrant golden pompom flowers in late winter, and sharp thorns. The fragrance in late winter is remarkable — one of the most perfumed native plants in SW Florida.
plants.attracts_specific: Honeybees (critical early spring nectar source), Native bees, Gulf fritillary butterfly, Cloudless sulphur butterfly, Nesting birds (protected by thorns)

seasonal_care.march: Flowering — peak fragrance. Peak bee activity. Do not prune.

common_problems.symptoms: Puncture wounds from thorns
common_problems.solution: Prevention through siting. Plant at least 6 ft from walkways and pet areas. Wear heavy gloves during any pruning.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries. Less common at big box stores.
plants.expert_tips: Sweet acacia blooms in late winter when virtually nothing else is flowering in SW Florida — it is a critical early-season food source for bees emerging from slower winter months. The fragrance is used in real perfumery — the species is one of the sources of cassie absolute, a traditional perfume ingredient.
plants.fun_fact: Sweet acacia (Vachellia farnesiana) is named for Cardinal Odoardo Farnese, who grew one in his Roman garden in the early 1600s. The fragrance is used in high-end perfumery and has been for centuries.
plants.traditional_uses: Used throughout history as a source of perfume (cassie absolute) and gum arabic. Pods and seeds eaten by indigenous peoples. Bark used medicinally.
plants.conservation_notes: A native of SW Florida's pine flatwood and scrub edges, sweet acacia populations have declined with habitat loss. Its thorns make it excellent wildlife habitat — small birds nest in the protected branches away from predators.

plants.description: One of the most spectacular flowering trees in the world — explosively covered in brilliant orange-red blooms in early summer. A defining tree of SW Florida's landscape. Fast-growing with a broad flat canopy providing excellent shade. Non-native but low ecological risk.
warnings: Mildly toxic to pets if large quantities of seeds are ingested — monitor pets around fallen seed pods.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect dry brown seed pods from the ground. Scarify seeds by nicking the hard coat with a knife or soaking in boiling water for 30 seconds then cool water for 24 hours. Sow 1 inch deep in well-drained mix.
plants.propagation_cutting: Difficult from cuttings — not recommended. Air layering works but is unnecessary given how easily it grows from seed.
plants.germination_method: Scarify (nick seed coat or hot water soak), then direct sow 1 inch deep.
plants.germination_notes: One of the fastest and most reliable tree seeds to germinate once scarified. Without scarification, germination is very slow and erratic. Seedlings grow extremely fast — can reach 6 feet in the first year in SW Florida.
plants.transplant_notes: Plant in full sun only. Needs room for its wide spreading canopy (40–60 feet wide at maturity). Keep away from driveways and structures — surface roots can lift pavement. Sandy well-drained soil preferred. Drought-tolerant once established.
plants.looks_like_notes: African tulip tree also has bright orange flowers but is invasive in Florida. Key difference: royal poinciana has finely divided fern-like compound leaves and flat spreading canopy; African tulip has large simple leaves and upright tulip-shaped flowers.
plants.attracts_specific: Ruby-throated hummingbird (flowers), Honeybee, Various native bee species, Baltimore oriole (migration, nesting material), Northern mockingbird (nesting in dense canopy)

seasonal_care.january: Tree is partially or fully leafless in cooler winters — normal. Large brown seed pods from last year still hanging. No action needed.
seasonal_care.february: Still bare or leafing out slowly. Good month to fertilize with slow-release palm/tree fertilizer if desired.
seasonal_care.march: Leaves flushing rapidly. Tree is preparing for bloom. Do not prune now — risk removing flower buds.
seasonal_care.april: Leaves full. First flower buds visible. Do not prune.
seasonal_care.may: Bloom approaching. In warmer years, first flowers open late May.
seasonal_care.june: PEAK BLOOM — the most spectacular month in SW Florida gardens. Entire canopy covered in orange-red flowers. No action needed except to enjoy it.
seasonal_care.july: Bloom fading. Seed pods forming and elongating. Some continued flowering possible.
seasonal_care.august: Large flat brown seed pods elongating — can reach 2 feet. Hurricane month — the wide flat canopy can catch wind.
seasonal_care.september: Pods maturing. Tree fully leafed and providing dense shade.
seasonal_care.october: Pods drying and rattling in the breeze. Good time to do any light structural pruning after bloom season ends.
seasonal_care.november: Best month to plant new royal poinciana. Pods can be collected for seed propagation.
seasonal_care.december: Tree going briefly deciduous. Falling pods and leaves — some cleanup needed.

common_problems.symptoms: Tree leafs out normally but produces no flowers or blooms very sparsely
common_problems.solution: Most common cause is overwatering or too much nitrogen fertilizer. Reduce irrigation and stop nitrogen fertilizers. A dry stress period before bloom season (March–May) triggers better flowering. Trees under 5 years rarely bloom well.

common_problems.symptoms: Cracked driveways, lifted sidewalks near mature trees
common_problems.solution: Prevention only — plant well away from pavement. No effective solution once roots are established under hardscape.

common_problems.symptoms: Large branches broken in storms, wide canopy acts as sail
common_problems.solution: Structural pruning to maintain a strong central leader and reduce canopy weight before hurricane season helps. Remove dead wood annually.

common_problems.symptoms: Premature leaf drop and cold-damaged branch tips after temperatures below 35°F
common_problems.solution: Royal poinciana is frost-sensitive. Cover young trees with frost cloth when temperatures below 35°F are forecast. Established large trees recover from light frost damage.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: One of the most widely available ornamental trees in SW Florida — found at virtually every nursery and big-box garden center. Very inexpensive from seed. Buy small container trees (3–7 gallon) for best transplant success.
plants.expert_tips: The key to spectacular blooming is dry stress. Royal poinciana blooms in response to the end of a dry season. In SW Florida, the natural dry season (January–May) followed by the rainy season (June) mimics this trigger perfectly. If you irrigate heavily year-round, you confuse the bloom signal. Let the tree go dry in spring and it will reward you with its best display.
plants.fun_fact: Royal poinciana is considered one of the most beautiful flowering trees in the world and is the national tree of Puerto Rico. In Madagascar where it originated it is now rare in the wild due to deforestation — meaning the trees lining SW Florida streets may represent one of the largest populations of the species on earth.
plants.traditional_uses: Not native to Florida — indigenous to Madagascar. In its native range and throughout the Caribbean, bark preparations were used medicinally for fever reduction. The hard wood is used for furniture and charcoal in Madagascar.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native but considered low ecological risk — does not naturalize aggressively in SW Florida. Ironically it is endangered in its native Madagascar while thriving as a landscape tree worldwide. No conservation concerns in Florida.

plants.description: Iconic tropical tree with intensely fragrant flowers in white, pink, yellow, red, and multicolor. One of the most planted ornamentals in SW Florida. Very drought tolerant. Goes briefly deciduous in winter.
warnings: Toxic to pets — milky sap causes vomiting, diarrhea, and skin irritation in dogs and cats. Keep pets away from fallen flowers and branches.
plants.propagation_seed: Seeds found in paired pod 'horns' that split open when ripe. Sow fresh seeds with papery wing attached, barely cover in sandy mix. Seedlings take 3–5 years to bloom and flower color is unpredictable from seed.
plants.propagation_cutting: The standard method — extremely easy. Cut a branch tip 12–18 inches long, let the cut end dry in shade for 1–2 weeks until the sap seals completely. Then plant 3–4 inches deep in well-drained sandy mix. Do not water for the first 2 weeks after planting — this forces the cutting to develop roots rather than rotting. Roots in 4–8 weeks.
plants.germination_method: Surface sow fresh seeds in sandy mix, barely cover.
plants.germination_notes: Seeds viable only when fresh. Old dry seeds germinate poorly. Use cuttings from a known variety to reproduce specific colors and fragrance.
plants.transplant_notes: One of the easiest trees to move — plumeria can be dug up, let dry out for a week, and replanted with high success. Full sun is essential. Excellent drainage required — plumeria rots quickly in wet soil. Sandy soil is ideal. Can be grown in large containers. Protect from frost — move container plants indoors when temps drop below 32°F.
plants.looks_like_plants: Cecropia (Cecropia palmata), Papaya (Carica papaya) when young
plants.looks_like_notes: Plumeria is fairly distinctive with its thick succulent-like branches and milky sap when broken. The clustered leaves at branch tips and characteristic forked branching pattern make it identifiable even without flowers.
plants.attracts_specific: Frangipani hawkmoth / tetrio sphinx (Pseudosphinx tetrio) — primary caterpillar host, Ruby-throated hummingbird (flowers), Snowberry clearwing moth, Various sphinx moths (night pollinators), Zebra longwing butterfly (occasional nectar)

seasonal_care.january: Tree is leafless — completely normal. Do not water. Do not fertilize. This is the dormant rest period the tree needs.
seasonal_care.february: Still leafless. Resist the urge to water or assume the tree is dead. Check by scratching bark — if green underneath, it is alive.
seasonal_care.march: First leaf buds swell and open. Begin watering again as leaves emerge. Resume monthly fertilization.
seasonal_care.april: Leaves expanding rapidly. First flower buds visible at branch tips. Fertilize with high-phosphorus fertilizer to boost bloom.
seasonal_care.may: Peak early bloom season begins. Water deeply once or twice a week. Great time to plant new plumerias.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — reduce supplemental irrigation. Blooming continues through summer. Watch for rust disease on leaves.
seasonal_care.july: Heavy summer bloom. Rust disease (orange powdery spores under leaves) common but usually not fatal. Remove heavily affected leaves.
seasonal_care.august: Continued blooming. Hurricane month — plumeria branches are brittle and prone to breakage in storms.
seasonal_care.september: Blooming continues. Any broken branches from storms can be replanted as cuttings.
seasonal_care.october: Blooming slowing as days shorten. Begin reducing water.
seasonal_care.november: Leaves yellowing and dropping — completely normal. Stop fertilizing. Reduce watering to nothing.
seasonal_care.december: Fully dormant. Do not water at all. Cold-sensitive — protect from frost below 32°F.

common_problems.symptoms: Bright orange-yellow powdery pustules on undersides of leaves, premature leaf drop
common_problems.solution: Very common in SW Florida's humid summers. Remove and dispose of heavily infected leaves. Spray with sulfur or copper fungicide as preventive. Rust is unsightly but rarely kills established trees. Choose rust-resistant varieties when purchasing.

common_problems.symptoms: Black rotting tip of branches, soft blackened stem tissue progressing downward
common_problems.solution: Cut back to healthy tissue well below the rot. Let cut dry completely before watering. Caused by Phytophthora — avoid overhead watering and overwatering.

common_problems.symptoms: Large black and yellow striped caterpillars rapidly defoliating branches
common_problems.solution: Handpick if tree is small. Large healthy trees recover easily. Spray with Bt if defoliation is severe on young trees. The moths are beautiful and worth tolerating if you can.

common_problems.symptoms: Tree leafs out but never blooms or stopped blooming
common_problems.solution: Most common cause is insufficient sun — plumeria needs 6+ hours of direct sun daily. Second cause is too much nitrogen fertilizer. Switch to a high-phosphorus fertilizer (higher middle number like 10-30-10).

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Extremely widely available at all SW Florida nurseries, big-box garden centers, and farmers markets. Local plumeria societies (Florida Plumeria Council has SW Florida members) are excellent sources for unusual varieties with guaranteed colors.
plants.expert_tips: The number one mistake with plumeria in SW Florida is watering during dormancy. When the tree drops its leaves in winter, stop watering completely — wet soil during dormancy causes root rot that kills the tree. The second mistake is planting in partial shade. Plumeria in anything less than full sun will be a leafy non-blooming disappointment. For best fragrance, the classic white/yellow varieties are consistently the most intensely fragrant.
plants.fun_fact: Plumeria flowers produce fragrance to attract hawkmoths for pollination but offer the moths no nectar in return — it is a purely deceptive relationship. The flowers advertise a reward that does not exist, and the moths are repeatedly fooled into visiting flower after flower, transferring pollen in the process.
plants.traditional_uses: Sacred in many Asian and Pacific Island cultures — used in Hawaiian leis, Buddhist and Hindu temple offerings, and Mexican Day of the Dead altars. In traditional Caribbean medicine, bark preparations were used for venereal disease treatments. The fragrant oil is used extensively in perfumery.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental with no invasive concerns in Florida. The frangipani hawkmoth caterpillar (a spectacular black and yellow striped caterpillar) is a notable visitor that depends on plumeria as its primary host plant in SW Florida.
