plants.description: Spectacular flowering trees that put on a jaw-dropping show of pink, yellow, or white trumpet blooms in spring — often before the leaves emerge. Bees and hummingbirds visit the flowers. Drought tolerant once established.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect papery winged seeds from pods before they fully open and blow away. Sow fresh seeds on surface of sandy mix, barely cover. Germination is fast and reliable from fresh seed.
plants.propagation_cutting: Possible from semi-hardwood cuttings in summer with rooting hormone, but seed is easier and more reliable.
plants.germination_method: Surface sow fresh seeds in sandy mix, barely cover.
plants.germination_notes: Seeds lose viability quickly — sow as soon as possible after collecting. Seedlings may take 5–8 years to first bloom. Grafted nursery trees bloom sooner.
plants.transplant_notes: Plant in full sun — tabebuia will not bloom well in shade. Well-drained soil required. Drought-tolerant once established. Water weekly for first year. Most commonly available species in SW Florida are T. heterophylla (pink), T. caraiba (yellow), and T. bahamensis (white).
plants.looks_like_plants: African tulip tree (Spathodea campanulata), Jacaranda (Jacaranda mimosifolia)
plants.looks_like_notes: African tulip tree (invasive!) has orange-red tubular flowers — very different from tabebuia's trumpet-shaped flowers. Jacaranda has purple-blue flowers and similar fine compound leaves. When in doubt, flower color and shape are the easiest identifiers.
plants.attracts_specific: Ruby-throated hummingbird (primary flower visitor), Honeybee, Bumblebee, Various native bee species, Baltimore oriole (migration — attracted to flowers)

seasonal_care.january: Tree may be partially leafless — normal for winter. No action needed. Flower buds are forming on bare branches.
seasonal_care.february: PEAK BLOOM for most species — flowers erupt on bare or nearly bare branches. One of SW Florida's most spectacular winter events.
seasonal_care.march: Bloom fading. Leaves emerging. Seed pods forming and elongating. No action needed.
seasonal_care.april: Full foliage. Papery seed pods releasing seeds. Light fertilization acceptable.
seasonal_care.may: Active growth. Water new plantings deeply through end of dry season.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — stop irrigation. Some secondary bloom possible on T. caraiba after rains.
seasonal_care.july: Full canopy providing excellent shade. No action needed.
seasonal_care.august: Good structural month — assess any pruning needs after bloom season is long past.
seasonal_care.september: Continued growth. Good month to plant new tabebuia.
seasonal_care.october: Growth slowing. Leaves beginning to thin on more deciduous species.
seasonal_care.november: Best planting month. Flower buds forming inside branches — do not prune.
seasonal_care.december: Leaf drop continuing on deciduous species. Flower buds maturing. Do not prune.

common_problems.symptoms: Tree is healthy and leafy but produces few or no flowers
common_problems.solution: Most common cause is insufficient drought stress — tabebuia blooms in response to dry season stress. Reduce or stop irrigation from November through the bloom period. Young trees under 5 years rarely bloom heavily.

common_problems.symptoms: White powdery coating on new leaves and shoots
common_problems.solution: Common in humid weather especially spring. Usually outgrown. Improve air circulation. Sulfur-based fungicide spray if needed.

common_problems.symptoms: Branch splitting or breakage at crotches during storms
common_problems.solution: Structural pruning to remove co-dominant stems and narrow V-crotches reduces storm risk. Do this when trees are young to develop a strong single-leader structure.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Widely available at SW Florida nurseries. Pink trumpet tree (T. heterophylla) is most common at big-box stores. For yellow (T. caraiba) and white (T. bahamensis) species, check specialty nurseries. Named grafted varieties bloom earlier and more reliably than seedlings.
plants.expert_tips: The bloom is triggered by dry season stress — the tree flowers in a burst of reproductive effort as it senses the end of drought. Heavy irrigation year-round suppresses flowering. Let tabebuia experience the natural SW Florida dry season and it will reward you. The show lasts only 1–2 weeks but the entire tree covered in flowers with no leaves visible is one of the greatest spectacles in SW Florida gardening.
plants.fun_fact: Tabebuia wood (commonly called 'ipe' or 'ironwood' in the lumber trade) is so dense and hard it sinks in water and is naturally rot-resistant for 25+ years without treatment. It is used for outdoor decking and boardwalks worldwide — including many US national park boardwalks.
plants.traditional_uses: Bark of various Tabebuia species has been used throughout Latin America as a treatment for cancer, fungal infections, and inflammatory conditions. Taheebo or pau d'arco tea is made from the inner bark and sold in health food stores. Research on lapachol compounds has shown some antimicrobial properties though clinical evidence is limited.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamentals with low invasive risk in Florida. Some Tabebuia species are considered threatened in their native Central American range due to deforestation. No conservation concerns in Florida landscape use.

plants.description: Very popular non-native with distinctive bright red brush-like flower spikes. Hummingbirds and bees adore the flowers. Drought and salt tolerant. Can be grown as a large shrub or trained into a multi-trunk tree up to 25 ft.
plants.propagation_seed: Tiny seeds in woody capsules that may remain on the plant for years. Collect older capsules, dry in paper bag, shake out seeds. Sow on surface of moist sandy mix, do not cover. Seeds germinate readily.
plants.propagation_cutting: Semi-hardwood cuttings in summer — take 4–6 inch cuttings, strip lower leaves, dip in rooting hormone, plant in sandy perlite mix, keep humid. Roots in 6–8 weeks.
plants.propagation_division: Not applicable for tree forms. Multi-stem shrub forms can be divided carefully.
plants.germination_method: Surface sow tiny seeds on moist mix, do not cover.
plants.germination_notes: Seed propagation produces variable results in terms of flower color and habit. Cuttings from a known plant are preferred for consistent results.
plants.transplant_notes: Very adaptable — tolerates most SW Florida soils including coastal sandy soils. Full sun is essential for best blooming. Tolerates brief flooding. Can be planted near saltwater. Water weekly for first 6 months, then drought-tolerant.
plants.looks_like_plants: Invasive Melaleuca / punk tree (Melaleuca quinquenervia), Tea tree (Leptospermum spp.)
plants.looks_like_notes: The invasive paper bark Melaleuca quinquenervia has similar narrow leaves but very different flowers and distinctive spongy papery bark in thick layers that peels in sheets — ornamental bottlebrush has regular firm bark.
plants.attracts_specific: Ruby-throated hummingbird (primary — red flowers are highly attractive), Rufous hummingbird (winter migrant, rare), Honeybee, Bumblebee, Various native bee species, Painted bunting (seeds, winter)

seasonal_care.january: Dry season. Established plants need no irrigation. Some varieties produce light winter bloom. No action needed.
seasonal_care.february: Good month to do any shaping — before the main spring bloom flush. Light fertilization if desired.
seasonal_care.march: Spring bloom begins — bright red brush flowers covering branch tips. No pruning during bloom.
seasonal_care.april: Peak spring bloom. Heavy hummingbird and bee activity. No action needed.
seasonal_care.may: Bloom fading. Woody seed capsules form along stems. Light pruning after bloom to shape and encourage a second flush.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — stop irrigation. Secondary bloom flush often follows pruning.
seasonal_care.july: Possible secondary bloom in summer. Fast growth during rainy season.
seasonal_care.august: Hurricane month — bottlebrush handles wind well due to flexible branches.
seasonal_care.september: Good time to plant new bottlebrush. Fall bloom possible.
seasonal_care.october: Some varieties bloom again in fall. Reduce irrigation for new plants.
seasonal_care.november: Best planting month. Light pruning acceptable.
seasonal_care.december: No action needed. Some late bloom possible in warm winters.

common_problems.symptoms: Swollen galls on stems, witches-broom of distorted growth, die-back
common_problems.solution: Prune affected stems well below galls. Sterilize pruning tools between cuts. No effective chemical control. Severely affected plants should be replaced.

common_problems.symptoms: Yellowing, wilting despite irrigation, death from base up
common_problems.solution: Though bottlebrush tolerates brief flooding, extended waterlogged soil causes root rot. Ensure good drainage for permanent plantings.

common_problems.symptoms: Crusty brown bumps on stems, sticky honeydew, sooty mold
common_problems.solution: Treat with horticultural oil spray in cooler months. Pruning heavily infested branches may be more practical on large plants.

common_problems.symptoms: Few flowers compared to previous years
common_problems.solution: Usually caused by heavy shade or over-fertilization with nitrogen. Ensure full sun. Switch to a low-nitrogen high-phosphorus fertilizer.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: One of the most widely available ornamental trees in SW Florida — found at all nurseries and big-box garden centers. Very inexpensive. Weeping bottlebrush (Callistemon viminalis / Melaleuca viminalis) is the most common variety sold locally.
plants.expert_tips: Note that the genus Callistemon has been reclassified — many plants sold as Callistemon are now technically Melaleuca in updated taxonomy. Do not confuse with the invasive Melaleuca quinquenervia (paper bark / punk tree) — a completely different species on Florida's invasive species list. After bloom, lightly prune the tips that just flowered — this removes woody seed capsules and encourages a new growth flush that will bloom again in 6–8 weeks, giving you multiple bloom cycles per year.
plants.fun_fact: Bottlebrush flowers have no petals — what looks like the colorful 'bristles' are actually the long stamens (the pollen-producing parts of the flower). The actual petals are tiny and inconspicuous. The tree is essentially one giant display of reproductive structures.
plants.traditional_uses: Non-native (Australian origin). Aboriginal Australians used various Callistemon species medicinally — leaves were crushed and inhaled for head colds and infusions used for skin ailments. The flexible branches were used for weaving. Not part of SW Florida's indigenous plant traditions.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native Australian ornamental with no invasive concerns in Florida. Excellent hummingbird and pollinator plant. The reclassification to Melaleuca may cause confusion at nurseries — verify you are not purchasing the invasive paper bark Melaleuca quinquenervia.

plants.description: Extremely popular ornamental tree with showy summer blooms in pink, red, white, and purple. Bees visit the flowers actively. Attractive peeling bark and fall color. Very drought tolerant. One of the most commonly planted trees in SW Florida.
warnings: Avoid heavy topping — it destroys the natural form and weakens the tree. Prune lightly or not at all.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect small seed pods in fall. Sow seeds in spring on surface of sandy mix. Germinate readily but flower color from seed is unpredictable.
plants.propagation_cutting: Easy from hardwood cuttings in late winter or softwood cuttings in summer. Take 6–8 inch cuttings, dip in rooting hormone, plant in moist sandy mix. Roots readily.
plants.propagation_division: Multi-stem clumps can be divided carefully in late winter before new growth.
plants.germination_method: Surface sow on moist sandy mix in spring.
plants.germination_notes: Seeds germinate easily but seedlings produce variable flower colors. For specific named colors, use cuttings from the parent plant.
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants easily. Full sun is essential — in shade it produces poor bloom and is very susceptible to powdery mildew. Plant in well-drained soil. Salt-sensitive — do not plant near coast or in salty soils. Water weekly for first year.
plants.looks_like_plants: Japanese crape myrtle (Lagerstroemia fauriei), Hybrid crape myrtles (L. indica x fauriei)
plants.looks_like_notes: Japanese crape myrtle (L. fauriei) is similar but has white flowers only and is more tree-like. Most plants sold in nurseries as crepe myrtle are actually L. indica x fauriei hybrids which combine the best traits of both and are generally preferred for better mildew resistance.
plants.attracts_specific: Honeybee, Bumblebee, Various native bee species, Hummingbird (occasional nectar), American goldfinch (seeds, winter), Dark-eyed junco (seeds, winter)

seasonal_care.january: Fully dormant and leafless — completely normal. Attractive seed heads and exfoliating bark visible. Do NOT prune now.
seasonal_care.february: Still dormant. Do not prune — wait until you see new growth buds swelling. If you must prune, late February is acceptable when buds show color.
seasonal_care.march: New growth buds swelling and opening. Light pruning of crossing branches acceptable only now. Begin fertilizing with slow-release fertilizer.
seasonal_care.april: Rapid leaf expansion. Flower buds forming. Do not prune — you will remove flower buds.
seasonal_care.may: Early bloomers beginning to flower. Excellent bee activity. No pruning.
seasonal_care.june: Peak summer bloom begins. Spectacular color. Deadhead spent flower clusters to encourage rebloom.
seasonal_care.july: Continued heavy bloom. Deadheading spent blooms extends flowering season through fall.
seasonal_care.august: Continued bloom. Hurricane month — crepe myrtle handles wind well due to flexible multi-stem structure.
seasonal_care.september: Bloom continuing into fall. Fall leaf color beginning to develop on some varieties.
seasonal_care.october: Bloom ending. Beautiful fall foliage color — orange, red, and yellow. One of SW Florida's best fall color plants.
seasonal_care.november: Leaves dropping. Do not prune yet — wait until late winter. Seed heads provide winter interest.
seasonal_care.december: Leafless dormancy. Attractive exfoliating bark visible. Do not prune.

common_problems.symptoms: White powdery coating on new leaves, distorted growth, poor flower development
common_problems.solution: SW Florida's humidity makes powdery mildew a constant issue on susceptible varieties. Choose mildew-resistant named varieties (Natchez, Tuscarora, Sioux, Acoma, Dynamite series). Ensure full sun and good air circulation. Treat with potassium bicarbonate or neem oil if needed.

common_problems.symptoms: Tree cut to ugly stubs annually, resulting in witches-broom regrowth, weak structure, disease susceptibility
common_problems.solution: Do not top crepe myrtles. Ever. Remove only crossing branches, suckers, and seed heads. If a tree is too large, replace it with a naturally smaller variety rather than annual topping.

common_problems.symptoms: Curled new leaves, sticky honeydew, sooty mold, clusters of small insects
common_problems.solution: Common in spring on new growth. Strong water spray knocks them off. Treat with insecticidal soap if severe. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides.

common_problems.symptoms: Angular brown spots on leaves, premature defoliation
common_problems.solution: Common in humid conditions. Rake and remove fallen leaves. Improve air circulation. Copper fungicide spray as preventive in wet months.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Found at every nursery and big-box garden center. For SW Florida, prioritize mildew-resistant varieties: Natchez (white, large), Tuscarora (coral-pink, large), Sioux (pink, medium), Acoma (white, semi-dwarf), Dynamite (red, large). Avoid unnamed seedlings — color and mildew resistance are unknown.
plants.expert_tips: Never top a crepe myrtle. This practice destroys the tree's natural vase shape, creates weak knobby regrowth that breaks in storms, and makes the tree perpetually susceptible to disease. If your crepe myrtle is 'too big,' you planted the wrong variety. SW Florida nurseries carry everything from dwarf 3-foot varieties to 30-foot trees — match the variety to the space.
plants.fun_fact: Crepe myrtle's exfoliating bark is one of the most beautiful bark textures of any ornamental tree — smooth patches of cream, cinnamon, and gray peel away to reveal fresh bark beneath. A mature multi-stem crepe myrtle with its twisted trunks and peeling bark is a genuine work of living sculpture in winter when fully leafless.
plants.traditional_uses: Native to China and Korea — not part of Florida indigenous traditions. Widely used in traditional Chinese medicine — bark preparations for antifungal and antimicrobial applications. Leaves used for fever and skin conditions in some Asian traditional medicine systems.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental with no invasive concerns in Florida. Moderate wildlife value — primarily bees during bloom. No conservation concerns.

plants.description: The king of SW Florida fruit trees. Thrives in Cape Coral's heat and humidity. Grafted trees fruit in 2-3 years. Prune annually after harvest to control size and promote production. Watch for anthracnose fungal disease during wet season.

varieties.notes: One of the best backyard varieties — compact tree, incredibly rich flavor, no fiber. Self-pollinating. Early harvest May-June.

varieties.name: Cogshall
varieties.notes: Top condo mango — slow growing, very easy to control size. Perfect for small yards or containers. Fiberless, excellent flavor.

varieties.name: Nam Doc Mai
varieties.notes: Thai variety with sweet fragrant fiber-free fruit. Semi-dwarf, manageable size. July-August harvest.

varieties.name: Kent
varieties.notes: Considered one of the sweetest Florida mangoes. Large tree but excellent production. Late season harvest July-August.

varieties.name: Keitt
varieties.notes: Best late season variety — stays green when ripe. Large fruit, heat tolerant, excellent disease resistance. Harvest August-September.

plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Excellent fruit tree for SW Florida in well-drained spots. West Indian varieties are best suited to Cape Coral's heat. Needs good drainage. Plant Type A and Type B varieties together for best pollination. Watch for laurel wilt disease.
warnings: Toxic to pets — the leaves, bark, skin, and pit contain persin which causes vomiting and diarrhea in dogs and cats. Keep fallen fruit picked up.

varieties.name: Choquette
varieties.notes: One of the most popular Florida backyard varieties. Large fruit up to 3 lbs, good flavor. Harvest November-January.

varieties.name: Monroe
varieties.notes: Large high-quality fruit with excellent flavor. Good disease resistance. Pairs well with Choquette for cross-pollination.

varieties.name: Brogdon
varieties.notes: Most cold-tolerant Florida variety. Medium fruit, good flavor. Harvest August-October.

varieties.name: Hall
varieties.notes: Excellent disease resistance — recommended by UF/IFAS. Good flavor, medium-large fruit. Harvest October-November.

varieties.name: Lula
varieties.notes: Classic Florida variety, cold tolerant, good production. Medium fruit with rich flavor. Harvest October-December.

plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: One of the best all-around wildlife shrubs for Southwest Florida. Tubular red-orange flowers bloom nearly year-round attracting hummingbirds and butterflies constantly. Dark berries eaten by many bird species. Host plant for the pluto sphinx moth. Important: only plant the true native Hamelia patens var. patens — not dwarf, African, or compacta varieties.
warnings: Do NOT buy dwarf, African, or compacta varieties — they are not native and have significantly less wildlife value.

water_needs_detail.established_frequency: None — SW Florida rainfall sufficient once established

plants.growth_notes: Can reach 6 ft in first season under ideal conditions
plants.pruning_notes: Hard prune in spring to maintain size and encourage dense bushy growth
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: One of the most forgiving native shrubs in SW Florida. Tolerates poor soil, drought, and neglect.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, supports 5+ wildlife categories, year-round host and nectar source
plants.propagation_seed: Collect ripe berries, clean pulp, sow fresh. Germination in 14-21 days.
plants.propagation_cutting: Softwood cuttings in spring-summer. Root in moist mix, 3-4 weeks.
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seed germinates best — viability drops quickly
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants easily from container. Water well for first 2-3 weeks. Avoid transplanting in peak summer heat — fall is ideal in SW Florida.
plants.looks_like_plants: African firebush (Hamelia patens var. glabra), dwarf firebush, compacta firebush
plants.looks_like_notes: Dwarf, African, and compacta varieties look similar but are not native and have significantly less wildlife value. Always verify you are buying Hamelia patens var. patens.
plants.attracts_specific: Pluto sphinx moth (Xylophanes pluto) — host plant; Ruby-throated hummingbird; Gulf fritillary butterfly; Zebra longwing butterfly

seasonal_care.january: No action needed. Enjoy winter blooms.
seasonal_care.february: Good time to prune if size control needed before spring flush.
seasonal_care.march: Apply slow-release fertilizer if desired. New growth begins.
seasonal_care.april: Monitor for whitefly — treat with neem oil if needed.
seasonal_care.may: Peak growing season begins. Water weekly if no rain for 2+ weeks.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season begins — typically no irrigation needed.
seasonal_care.july: Monitor for fungal issues in humid conditions. Remove dead wood.
seasonal_care.august: Continue monitoring. Peak wildlife activity on berries and flowers.
seasonal_care.september: Berries abundant — peak bird attraction. Excellent planting month.
seasonal_care.october: Best time to plant new specimens. Fall planting season begins.
seasonal_care.november: Continue fall planting. Prune lightly if needed.
seasonal_care.december: No action needed. Hardy through SW Florida winters.

common_problems.symptoms: Yellowing leaves, sticky residue, white insects under leaves
common_problems.solution: Spray with neem oil solution weekly for 3 weeks. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill beneficial insects visiting the flowers.

common_problems.symptoms: Long bare stems with foliage only at tips, reduced flowering
common_problems.solution: Hard prune to 12-18 inches in late winter or early spring. Will rebound vigorously with dense bushy growth within 6-8 weeks.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at most SW Florida native plant nurseries. Ensure you buy Hamelia patens var. patens — not dwarf or African variety.
plants.where_to_buy_local: FNPS plant sales, native plant nurseries throughout Lee and Collier counties
plants.expert_tips: The single most common mistake with firebush is buying the wrong variety — African and dwarf forms are widely sold but have a fraction of the wildlife value. The true native grows large — plan for 6-8 ft and prune hard once a year rather than clipping constantly. Hummingbirds will find it within days of planting if they are in the area.
plants.fun_fact: Firebush berries contain compounds studied for antimicrobial and antioxidant properties. The Seminole people used the plant medicinally.
plants.traditional_uses: Used medicinally by indigenous peoples of Central and South America. Berries used in traditional beverages in some cultures.
plants.conservation_notes: Populations of the true native firebush are declining in the landscape trade as non-native varieties dominate nursery stock. Buying and planting the true native variety actively supports genetic conservation of the species in SW Florida.
plants.hoa_notes: Many SW Florida HOAs now accept native plants. Lee and Collier County have native plant provisions.

plants.description: Famous for its extraordinary clusters of metallic purple berries eaten by over 40 bird species and deer. Host plant for spring azure butterfly. Low maintenance — dies back and rebounds vigorously each season. Adaptable to sun through shade.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Widely planted for extraordinary drought and salt tolerance, fast growth, and showy flowers in pink, white, red, and yellow. However the toxicity is severe and demands serious thought before planting in home landscapes with children or pets.
warnings: HIGHLY TOXIC — all parts including sap, flowers, leaves, stems, and water in a vase containing oleander are extremely toxic to humans, pets, horses, and livestock. Smoke from burning branches is toxic. One of the most dangerous common landscape plants.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: Many HOAs restrict or ban oleander due to toxicity concerns near children.

plants.description: One of the most essential hummingbird and butterfly plants for Southwest Florida. Brilliant red spikes bloom nearly year-round. Self-seeds prolifically so you will always have more. Very drought tolerant and easy. Excellent companion to firebush and blue porterweed.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Florida's single best lawn-substitute groundcover. Host plant for common buckeye, phaon crescent, and white peacock butterflies. Tiny white-purple flowers attract native bees constantly. Seeds eaten by birds. Can be mowed. Handles light foot traffic. One of the most ecologically valuable plants per square foot in all of Southwest Florida.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: One of the absolute best native vines for Southwest Florida. Tubular red and orange flowers bloom nearly year-round and hummingbirds are completely unable to resist them. Red berries eaten by birds. Well-behaved unlike invasive Japanese honeysuckle. A must-have for any hummingbird garden.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: One of the most beloved native grasses in Florida. In fall the clouds of airy pink-purple flower plumes are absolutely stunning — glowing in late afternoon light. Seeds eaten by birds. Dense clumps provide cover for ground birds and lizards. Plant in drifts for maximum impact.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: The single most recommended native aquatic plant for Southwest Florida's canals, ponds, and wet areas. Vivid violet-blue flower spikes bloom nearly year-round. Bees and butterflies visit constantly. Seeds eaten by ducks and water birds. Dense colonies provide critical fish habitat. Edible — seeds eaten like buckwheat, young leaves cooked like spinach.

water_needs_detail.established_frequency: Permanent water or saturated soil required

plants.growth_notes: Spreads readily by rhizomes to form dense beneficial colonies
plants.pruning_notes: Cut back to water level in late winter if needed to control spread. Division is easy and creates new plants.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: One of the most reliable and easy aquatic natives for SW Florida. Plant it in shallow water or saturated soil and it does the rest.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, year-round bloomer, supports bees, butterflies, birds, fish habitat, edible, and canal-bank stabilizer
plants.propagation_seed: Collect seed heads when brown. Direct sow in wet soil or shallow water.
plants.propagation_cutting: Division of rhizomes in spring or fall. Each division with roots will establish quickly.
plants.propagation_division: Easy — divide clumps in spring. Most practical propagation method.
plants.germination_notes: Seeds need consistently wet conditions to germinate. Division is easier and faster.
plants.transplant_notes: Plant rhizomes or divisions directly into wet soil or shallow water up to 12 inches deep. No special care needed — simply keep roots wet.
plants.looks_like_notes: Water hyacinth is invasive and looks superficially similar when not in bloom. Pickerelweed has a lance-shaped leaf with a heart-shaped base; water hyacinth has rounded inflated leaf stalks. Never plant water hyacinth.
plants.attracts_specific: Wood duck (seeds), Anhinga (nesting cover), Purple gallinule (nesting and foraging), Native bees including bumble bees, Long-tailed skipper butterfly

seasonal_care.january: No action needed. May die back slightly in coolest weather — will rebound.
seasonal_care.february: Division and replanting can be done now if needed.
seasonal_care.march: Growth resumes strongly. Good time to divide and spread.
seasonal_care.september: Seed heads forming — important bird food source.
seasonal_care.november: Good time to divide and replant.
seasonal_care.december: May slow slightly but typically evergreen in SW Florida.

common_problems.symptoms: Distorted new growth, sticky residue, clusters of small insects on stems
common_problems.solution: Strong spray of water knocks them off. Natural predators like lady beetles usually control them without intervention. Neem oil if persistent.

common_problems.symptoms: Expanding beyond intended planting area
common_problems.solution: Division and removal of outer rhizomes in spring or fall. Rhizomes are easy to pull. Regular division also creates plants to share or expand elsewhere.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries and aquatic plant specialists throughout SW Florida. Occasionally at big box garden centers.
plants.where_to_buy_local: FNPS plant sales, aquatic nurseries in Lee and Collier counties
plants.expert_tips: Plant pickerelweed in masses rather than as individual specimens — a dense colony of 10-20 plants along a canal bank does far more ecological work than a single specimen. The combination of pickerelweed, duck potato, and alligator flag creates a complete native aquatic edge that stabilizes the bank, filters runoff, and supports a full range of wildlife.
plants.fun_fact: Pickerelweed flowers are trimorphic — the species produces three different flower forms with different arrangements of stamens and pistils to encourage cross-pollination between plants. This is rare in the plant world.
plants.traditional_uses: Young leaf stalks and seeds were eaten by Native Americans. Seeds can be eaten raw or roasted and ground into flour. Young leaves are edible cooked like spinach.
plants.conservation_notes: Pickerelweed colonies along SW Florida's canals provide critical water filtration, removing excess nutrients from runoff before they enter larger water bodies. Replacing invasive aquatic plants with pickerelweed actively improves water quality throughout the canal system.

plants.description: The most iconic epiphyte of the American South. Not a moss, not a parasite — a true flowering bromeliad. Critical nesting material for northern parulas, Baltimore orioles, and other birds. Indicator of clean air quality. Harmless to healthy trees. A living symbol of authentic Florida.
warnings: Spanish moss often harbors chiggers and redbugs — wear long sleeves and gloves when handling fresh fallen clumps.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Florida's most common native cactus and an ecological powerhouse. Large showy yellow flowers with red centers attract bees and butterflies. Red-purple fruits eaten by gopher tortoises, birds, deer, and small mammals. Entire plant is edible — pads, fruits, and flowers all used in cooking. Very drought and salt tolerant.
warnings: Glochids — tiny barbed bristles on pads and fruits — cause intense skin irritation and are nearly invisible. Always wear thick gloves when handling.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Florida's largest native terrestrial fern — bold arching fronds can reach 6-8 ft creating a dramatic tropical statement. Excellent groundcover under trees and in shaded areas. Provides dense wildlife cover for frogs, lizards, and ground birds. Very fast growing once established. Pet safe.
warnings: Do NOT confuse with invasive tuberous sword fern (N. cordifolia) or Asian sword fern (N. brownii). Native giant sword fern has double-toothed pinnae margins and no tubers on runners. Always verify scientific name at purchase.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: One of Southwest Florida's most magical native plants — white to pink lily flowers appear seemingly overnight after summer rains. Bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds visit the flowers. Naturalizes beautifully in lawns and garden beds spreading over time. A classic Florida native experience.
warnings: All parts toxic to humans and pets — bulbs especially dangerous containing lycorine alkaloids. Do not ingest.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Arguably the single most ecologically important weed in Florida. Butterflies and native bees swarm it constantly all year long — documented as one of the top three most important honeybee plants in the Southeast. Seeds eaten by birds. Edible leaves and flowers used as salad garnish. Let it grow wherever you can.
plants.management: Let grow freely or manage after blooming to limit spread. Worth keeping in every yard.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: The single most destructive invasive plant in Southwest Florida. Forms impenetrable dense thickets that completely displace native vegetation. Red berries look attractive but are mildly toxic and the tree provides almost no native wildlife value compared to the habitat it destroys. Now covers over 700,000 acres in South Florida. Remove immediately whenever found.
warnings: Sap causes severe skin and eye irritation — related to poison ivy. Wear gloves, eye protection, and long sleeves when handling. Berries toxic to pets. Smoke from burning is toxic.
plants.removal_method: Cut stems at ground level and immediately apply concentrated herbicide (triclopyr or glyphosate) to cut surface. DO NOT burn — smoke is toxic. Repeat treatments needed. Root system must be killed or it resprouts. Contact Lee or Collier County Extension for assistance.
plants.growth_notes: Extremely fast growing — can form dense thickets within 2-3 years if not immediately controlled
plants.pruning_notes: DO NOT PRUNE — cutting without immediately treating cut surface with herbicide causes vigorous resprouting
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Grows easily in any condition — this is part of why it is so destructive as an invasive.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Category 1 invasive. No native wildlife value. Actively destroys native habitat.
plants.germination_notes: Self-seeds prolifically — birds spread seeds throughout natural areas
plants.transplant_notes: DO NOT TRANSPLANT — invasive species. Remove and destroy all plants.
do_not_plant_near: This IS the plant to avoid — remove from property immediately
plants.looks_like_plants: Florida holly (common name used for this plant), Christmas berry
plants.looks_like_notes: Often sold under misleading common names like 'Florida holly.' The compound leaves with a distinctive turpentine smell when crushed, red berries in dense clusters, and rough gray bark are identifying features. If you smell turpentine when you crush a leaf — it is Brazilian pepper. Remove it.
plants.attracts_specific: Birds eat the berries and spread seeds into natural areas — this is how it spreads so effectively. The wildlife value does not offset the ecological damage.

seasonal_care.january: Remove any plants found on property.
seasonal_care.february: Remove any plants found on property.
seasonal_care.march: Remove any plants found on property. Spring flush makes new seedlings visible.
seasonal_care.april: Check for new seedlings from winter berry drop.
seasonal_care.may: Remove any plants found on property.
seasonal_care.june: Remove any plants found on property.
seasonal_care.july: Remove any plants found on property.
seasonal_care.august: Berries forming — remove before they ripen to prevent bird spread.
seasonal_care.september: Berries ripening — highest spread risk. Remove urgently.
seasonal_care.october: Peak berry production — urgent removal priority.
seasonal_care.november: Remove any plants found on property.
seasonal_care.december: Berries being consumed and spread by birds — check property for seedlings.

common_problems.symptoms: Vigorous new growth from cut stumps and roots within weeks of removal
common_problems.solution: Cut must be immediately treated with concentrated triclopyr or glyphosate applied directly to the cut surface within 60 seconds of cutting. Untreated cuts resprout more vigorously than before.

common_problems.problem: Skin and eye irritation during removal
common_problems.symptoms: Redness, burning, swelling from contact with sap
common_problems.solution: Wear gloves, long sleeves, eye protection, and closed shoes during all removal work. Wash exposed skin immediately with soap and water. Related to poison ivy — some people have severe reactions.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: DO NOT PURCHASE. Illegal to plant in Florida. If seen for sale, report to Florida Department of Agriculture.
plants.expert_tips: The most important thing to know: never cut Brazilian pepper without immediately treating the stump. A cut stump without herbicide will resprout 3-5 new stems for every one you cut — making the problem worse. Always have your herbicide ready before you make the first cut. Small seedlings under 12 inches can be pulled by hand — the root system is shallow when young.
plants.fun_fact: Brazilian pepper is related to cashew, mango, and poison ivy — all members of the Anacardiaceae family. This is why the sap causes skin irritation similar to poison ivy in sensitive individuals.
plants.traditional_uses: Used as a folk remedy in South America for various ailments — however the allergenic properties make self-treatment dangerous. Not recommended under any circumstances.
plants.conservation_notes: Brazilian pepper now covers over 700,000 acres of South Florida — more than any other invasive plant in the state. It costs Florida millions of dollars per year to control. Every plant removed from a private property directly contributes to protecting what remains of SW Florida's native ecosystems.

plants.description: Australian tree that has invaded over 500,000 acres of South Florida's wetlands. Drains wetlands by transpiring enormous amounts of water, converting sawgrass marshes and cypress swamps into melaleuca monocultures. Federally listed noxious weed. Remove immediately.
warnings: Do not burn standing melaleuca — heat triggers seed release from the canopy. One tree can release millions of seeds when burned.
plants.removal_method: Cut and immediately treat stump with concentrated herbicide. Hack and squirt method effective on larger trees. Biological control (Melaleuca snout beetle) available — contact SFWMD for current programs.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Free-floating plant from South America that can double its population in two weeks, completely choking canals, ponds, and waterways. Reduces oxygen in water killing fish. Blocks boat traffic. Has infested Florida waterways since the 1880s and costs the state millions annually to control. Never introduce to water features.
warnings: Removal requires permits for aquatic herbicide use in Florida waterways. Contact SFWMD before applying any chemical treatment to canals.
plants.removal_method: Physical removal by hand or equipment for small infestations. Aquatic herbicides (2,4-D, glyphosate labeled for aquatic use) for larger infestations — requires permits. Contact SFWMD for assistance with canal infestations.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification

plants.description: Underused native understory tree related to blueberry. Delicate bell-shaped white spring flowers feed bees. Shiny blue-black fall berries attract birds. Bark flakes to reveal attractive reddish layers. Well adapted to Florida's sandy soils.
plants.growth_notes: Slow growing understory tree
plants.pruning_notes: Light shaping only. Does not require regular pruning.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Requires acidic sandy soil — fails in alkaline conditions common in SW Florida. Test soil before planting.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, bee forage, bird berries, attractive bark
plants.propagation_seed: Collect berries when ripe. Clean and sow in acidic sandy mix.
plants.germination_method: Sow in acidic sandy mix — pH critical
plants.germination_notes: Needs acidic conditions for germination. Alkaline water inhibits germination.
plants.transplant_notes: Requires acidic well-drained sandy soil. Amend planting hole with sulfur and peat to lower pH. Test soil pH before planting. Mulch with pine bark.
do_not_plant_near: Alkaline soil areas without pH amendment
plants.looks_like_notes: Sparkleberry has smaller leaves and more tree-like growth habit than blueberry. The distinctive flaking reddish bark on older specimens is identifying. Berries are smaller and less flavorful than cultivated blueberry.
plants.attracts_specific: Various thrushes (berries), Eastern bluebird (berries), Native bees (spring flowers)

seasonal_care.february: Flowering begins — small white bell-shaped flowers

common_problems.symptoms: Yellow leaves, stunted growth
common_problems.solution: Almost always caused by soil pH too high. Sparkleberry requires acidic soil (4.5-6.5). Apply sulfur to lower pH and use acidifying fertilizer. This is the most common reason sparkleberry fails in SW Florida landscapes.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries. Requires acidic soil — confirm your site is appropriate before purchasing.
plants.expert_tips: Sparkleberry is rarely planted but genuinely beautiful especially in older specimens with their distinctive flaking reddish bark. The spring flowers are delicate and beautiful, the fall berries attract birds, and the bark provides year-round interest. Worth the extra effort of soil preparation.
plants.fun_fact: Sparkleberry is in the same genus as blueberries, huckleberries, and cranberries. The berries are edible but extremely astringent — they are essentially left to wildlife, which suits them perfectly.
plants.traditional_uses: Berries used in folk medicine as an astringent. Wood used for small tool handles by some Native American peoples.
plants.conservation_notes: One of the few native acid-soil plants of SW Florida's scrub and flatwood habitats. These ecosystems are among the most threatened in the state.

plants.description: Native coastal hammock tree with clusters of small grape-like fruits beloved by white-crowned pigeons and mockingbirds. Edible for humans — small and tart. Very salt and drought tolerant.
plants.growth_notes: Moderate growth. Slower than sea grape.
plants.pruning_notes: Can be maintained as a specimen tree or large shrub.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Very easy in coastal SW Florida. Extremely salt and drought tolerant.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, bird food critical for white-crowned pigeons, mammals, coastal habitat
plants.propagation_seed: Collect ripe purple berries. Clean and sow fresh.
plants.germination_method: Sow fresh cleaned seed in sandy mix
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seed much better than dried.
plants.transplant_notes: Very easy to transplant. Tolerates coastal exposure well.
plants.looks_like_notes: Pigeon plum has smaller, narrower leaves than sea grape. The bark is rougher and more textured. Smaller growth habit. Fruit clusters are similar but smaller.
plants.attracts_specific: White-crowned pigeon (primary consumer — critical food source), Mockingbird, Raccoon
plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries. Less common than sea grape.
plants.expert_tips: Pigeon plum is specifically named for the white-crowned pigeon — a beautiful bird that has experienced significant population declines as its coastal hammock food sources have been reduced by development. Planting pigeon plum is a direct conservation action for this species.
plants.fun_fact: White-crowned pigeons, which depend heavily on pigeon plum fruit, fly up to 100 miles daily between their nesting grounds in the Florida Keys and feeding areas on the mainland. Each pigeon plum planted in SW Florida is a potential refueling stop on this remarkable daily journey.
plants.traditional_uses: Fruit edible for humans — tart and small but palatable. Used in jams in some Caribbean cultures.
plants.conservation_notes: White-crowned pigeon populations have declined significantly with the loss of coastal hammock habitat. Pigeon plum is one of their most important food sources.

plants.description: Attractive native hammock tree with glossy pinnate leaves and clusters of small purple-black fruits that many birds eat. Fast-growing and good for quick canopy. Interesting compound leaves give a tropical appearance.
plants.growth_notes: Fast growing native hammock tree
plants.pruning_notes: Minimal pruning. Remove dead wood only.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Fast growing and low maintenance in well-drained sites.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, bird and mammal food from fruits, fast canopy establishment
plants.propagation_seed: Collect ripe purple-black fruits. Clean and sow fresh.
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seed germinates readily.
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants well from container. Fast growing once established.
plants.looks_like_notes: The compound pinnate leaves and clusters of small purple-black fruits on reddish stalks are identifying. Attractive tropical appearance year-round.
plants.attracts_specific: Migratory warblers (fruit), Northern mockingbird, Various frugivorous birds
plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at select native plant nurseries. Worth seeking out for fast canopy establishment.
plants.expert_tips: Paradise tree is one of the best native trees for quickly establishing a canopy in a restoration planting or new landscape. Its fast growth combined with genuine wildlife value makes it an excellent choice when immediate results are needed.
plants.fun_fact: The seeds of Simarouba glauca contain 55-70% oil and have been researched extensively as a biodiesel crop in tropical regions. The oil quality rivals olive oil for cooking.
plants.traditional_uses: Seeds are pressed for edible oil in Central America and India. The oil is also used medicinally and for soap making.
plants.conservation_notes: A tree of tropical hammocks increasingly rare in SW Florida due to habitat loss.

plants.description: Often overlooked but highly valuable native coastal hammock tree. Small red fruits are an important food source for migrating warblers and vireos. One of the few native trees that tolerates shade well. Very salt tolerant.
plants.growth_notes: Slow growing coastal hammock tree
plants.pruning_notes: Minimal pruning needed. Tolerates shaping.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Excellent once established but slow growing and specific to well-drained sites.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, migratory bird fruit, nesting, shade tolerant — rare trait in coastal natives
plants.propagation_seed: Collect red fruits when soft. Clean and sow fresh in well-drained mix.
plants.germination_method: Sow fresh cleaned seed in sandy mix
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seed performs much better than stored.
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants reasonably well from container. Plant in well-drained site. Tolerates partial shade — unusual for coastal species.
plants.looks_like_notes: Blolly identified by its small oval leaves, reddish new growth, and bright red berry clusters attractive to birds. The shade tolerance distinguishes it from most coastal natives.
plants.attracts_specific: Migratory warblers (red berries critical during fall migration), Red-bellied woodpecker, Gray catbird

seasonal_care.august: Berries ripening — peak migrant bird activity

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at select native plant nurseries. Often overlooked but highly recommended by Lee County Extension.
plants.expert_tips: Blolly is specifically recommended by the Lee County Extension as an underused native for coastal SW Florida landscapes. Its shade tolerance makes it invaluable for planting in the understory of larger coastal trees.
plants.fun_fact: Blolly is listed as a 'bird magnet' by the Florida Ornithological Society during fall migration. The red berries ripen precisely when migratory warblers and other migrants are moving through SW Florida.
plants.traditional_uses: Limited documented traditional uses.
plants.conservation_notes: A declining component of SW Florida's coastal hammock habitat. Each planted specimen contributes to preserving this tree in the landscape.

plants.description: Enormously productive in SW Florida. Leaves, pods, seeds, and flowers all edible and highly nutritious. Grows extremely fast. Straight trunks useful as garden stakes. Prune hard regularly to keep productive and manageable.
warnings: Leaves typically eaten cooked or dried rather than raw in large quantities.
plants.propagation_seed: One of the easiest trees to grow from seed. Plant fresh seeds (or dried seeds within 1 year) 1 inch deep in sandy well-drained mix. No pretreatment needed. Can be direct-sown in the ground.
plants.propagation_cutting: Very easy from large stem cuttings 1–2 inches in diameter, 3–5 feet long. Plant directly in ground, burying 1/3 of the cutting. Water once. Roots readily in warm months. This is the fastest way to establish a producing tree.
plants.germination_method: Direct sow 1 inch deep in sandy mix or in ground.
plants.germination_notes: Some of the fastest germination of any tree — seedlings often emerge in a week. Sandy well-drained soil is critical — moringa seedlings rot instantly in wet soil.
plants.transplant_notes: Moringa has a fragile taproot and transplants poorly from bare root once established. Direct sow or plant container seedlings while small. Excellent drainage is critical — moringa will die quickly in waterlogged soil. Full sun only. Space 10–15 feet apart if planting multiple trees, or 4–6 feet for a dense manageable hedge row.
plants.looks_like_notes: Young moringa with its small compound leaves can superficially resemble various Cassia/Senna species. The distinctive long thin seed pods (12–18 inches, triangular cross-section) are unmistakable on mature plants. Moringa leaves have a characteristic mild horseradish-mustard scent when crushed.
plants.attracts_specific: Ruby-throated hummingbird (flowers), Various bee species (nectar-rich flowers), Painted bunting (seeds), American goldfinch (seeds, winter), Various hawk moth species (pollinator)

seasonal_care.january: Dry season — water every 1–2 weeks. Tree may look sparse or drop some leaves in cooler weather — normal. Good month to harvest leaves for drying.
seasonal_care.february: Still cool and dry. Possible cold damage on young trees below 32°F — cover if frost forecast. Light pruning to shape acceptable.
seasonal_care.march: Growth accelerating as temperatures rise. Heavy flush of new leaves. Begin regular fertilization. Flowering resumes if it paused in winter.

seasonal_care.july: Peak growth. Harvest leaves, flowers, and young pods regularly. Heavy harvesting actually encourages bushier productive regrowth.

common_problems.problem: Root rot in wet or clay soil
common_problems.symptoms: Yellowing, wilting despite watering, soft rotting at base, sudden death
common_problems.solution: Moringa is native to dry tropical regions and is extremely intolerant of wet soil. This is the #1 cause of death in SW Florida. Plant only in well-drained sandy soil. Raised beds work well. No recovery once root rot is established.

common_problems.symptoms: Blackened wilted foliage after temperatures below 32°F, die-back to ground
common_problems.solution: In zone 9b, moringa may die back to the ground in a hard freeze. It typically regrows vigorously from the roots in spring. Mulch the root zone heavily before cold snaps.

common_problems.symptoms: Leaves stripped or skeletonized
common_problems.solution: Light damage is tolerable — the tree grows back so fast it usually outpaces the damage. Spray with Bt for heavier infestations. Avoid systemic insecticides on a food tree.

common_problems.symptoms: Curled new leaves, sticky honeydew, clusters of small insects
common_problems.solution: Common on tender new growth. Strong water spray dislodges most colonies. Insecticidal soap if severe.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Increasingly available at SW Florida nurseries and farmers markets. Seeds are widely available online and very inexpensive. Try local ethnic grocery stores serving Indian or Caribbean communities — they often carry moringa plants or know local growers.
plants.expert_tips: The single most important practice for moringa in SW Florida is regular aggressive pruning. Left unpruned it becomes a scraggly 20-foot tree with all the leaves and pods out of reach. Cut it back to 3–4 feet every few months and it stays a bushy 6–8 foot highly productive food shrub you can actually harvest easily. The more you harvest the leaves, the more it produces.
plants.fun_fact: Moringa seeds can be used to purify water — crushed seeds release proteins that cause suspended clay particles and bacteria to clump together and settle out, clarifying turbid water. This low-tech water purification method is actively used in developing countries as an alternative to chemical treatment.
plants.traditional_uses: One of the most extensively used medicinal and food plants in South and Southeast Asian traditions. Every part is used: leaves as a vegetable and nutritional supplement; seeds for cooking oil and water purification; roots used as a condiment similar to horseradish; pods cooked as a vegetable in Indian cuisine (drumstick curry); flowers eaten in salads and fritters.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native, originally from northern India. No invasive concerns in Florida. Increasingly popular as a home food forest tree and nutritional supplement crop in SW Florida. Its extreme productivity in our climate makes it one of the most food-secure trees you can plant in a SW Florida edible landscape.

plants.description: Stunning ornamental tree with large orchid-like purple-pink flowers that bloom in fall and winter — a welcome burst of color when little else is blooming. Sterile hybrid so does not set seed — no invasive risk. Very popular in SW Florida landscapes.
plants.growth_notes: Moderate growth ornamental tree
plants.pruning_notes: Light pruning to maintain shape. Sterile so no seed cleaning needed.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Easy and low maintenance. Sterile so no messy seed pods.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Non-native, bee and hummingbird forage, beautiful fall-winter bloomer
plants.propagation_seed: Sterile hybrid — does not produce viable seed. Propagate by grafting or air layering.
plants.germination_notes: Sterile hybrid cannot be propagated by seed. Buy grafted nursery stock.
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants well from container. Full to partial sun. Not salt tolerant — inland sites.
plants.looks_like_notes: Hong Kong orchid tree identified by its distinctive butterfly-shaped two-lobed leaves and large orchid-like purple-pink flowers. Sterile — produces no seed pods, unlike weedy Bauhinia species.
plants.attracts_specific: Honeybees, Hummingbirds, Native bees
plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at most SW Florida nurseries.
plants.expert_tips: Hong Kong orchid tree blooms when almost nothing else does — its fall and winter flowering season fills the gap left by summer-blooming plants. Combined with its butterfly-shaped leaves and orchid-like flowers it is one of the most distinctive landscape trees available.
plants.fun_fact: Hong Kong orchid tree was discovered in 1880 as a single tree growing near an abandoned house site in Hong Kong. It is a sterile hybrid of two other Bauhinia species that occurred naturally. Every Hong Kong orchid tree on earth is a clone descended from that single wild discovery.
plants.traditional_uses: No significant traditional uses.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental. The sterile nature means no invasive seed dispersal — making it more ecologically responsible than seeding Bauhinia species.

plants.description: Iconic symmetrical conifer widely planted in SW Florida as a living Christmas tree and landscape specimen. Very salt tolerant. Birds nest in the branches and eat seeds from cones. Grows tall and narrow — good for tight spaces.
warnings: Mildly toxic to cats and dogs — can cause vomiting and lethargy if needles are ingested.
plants.growth_notes: Moderate grower. Maintains its symmetrical form naturally.
plants.pruning_notes: Never prune the central leader — this destroys the tree's natural form permanently. Remove only dead branches.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Easy and essentially maintenance free in SW Florida. Very salt tolerant.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Non-native, bird nesting in branches, seed food from cones
plants.propagation_seed: Collect seeds from cones when ripe. Sow fresh in well-drained mix.
plants.propagation_cutting: Not practical — grows true from seed but slow.
plants.germination_method: Sow fresh seed in well-drained mix
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seed germinates better than stored.
plants.transplant_notes: Container trees transplant well. Very salt tolerant — good for coastal sites. Never remove the central leader.
do_not_plant_near: Do not remove central leader — permanently ruins the tree's form
plants.looks_like_notes: Norfolk Island pine identified by its distinctive perfectly symmetrical layered branch pattern. Horizontal branches in distinct whorls, soft short dark green needles. Unmistakable in landscape.
plants.attracts_specific: Various birds (nesting), Seed-eating birds from cones

seasonal_care.january: Good container or outdoor landscape performer

common_problems.symptoms: Lower branches dying back progressively
common_problems.solution: Normal aging process as tree grows — lower branches naturally die as the tree matures. Remove only when fully dead. Do not cut live lower branches prematurely.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available everywhere in SW Florida. One of the most commonly sold plants in the region.
plants.expert_tips: Norfolk Island pine is sold by the millions as living Christmas trees in the US. After Christmas, many end up in the landscape — they can eventually grow 50-100 ft tall. Consider the eventual size before planting one from your holiday display.
plants.fun_fact: Norfolk Island pines are not true pines — they belong to an ancient family that has remained essentially unchanged for over 200 million years. They were used by early Pacific navigators to identify Norfolk Island from far at sea.
plants.traditional_uses: The seeds of Norfolk Island pine were eaten by indigenous peoples of Norfolk Island. The wood is used for furniture and construction in the Pacific.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental widely planted in SW Florida. No significant invasive concerns.

plants.description: Tropical tree with intensely fragrant yellow-green star-shaped flowers used in perfumery — the scent is extraordinary. Blooms nearly year-round. Bees and hummingbirds visit. Grows very fast into a large weeping-form tree.
plants.growth_notes: Very fast growing tropical tree
plants.pruning_notes: Prune regularly to control size and shape. Can be maintained as a smaller specimen with pruning.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Fast growing but requires some care for best fragrance production.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Non-native, bee and hummingbird forage, extraordinary fragrance
plants.propagation_cutting: Semi-hardwood cuttings root in warm humid conditions.
plants.germination_notes: Cuttings the standard method.
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants well from container. Plant inland — not salt tolerant. Protect from cold below 40F.
plants.looks_like_notes: The weeping habit with branches that hang gracefully and the distinctive star-shaped greenish-yellow flowers with extraordinary fragrance are identifying features.
plants.attracts_specific: Honeybees, Hummingbirds
plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at specialty tropical nurseries. Less common at general garden centers.
plants.expert_tips: Ylang ylang fragrance is most intense in the evening and early morning. Plant near a patio, window, or walkway used in the evenings for maximum impact. The fragrance dissipates quickly in the midday heat.
plants.fun_fact: Ylang ylang is one of the most important fragrance ingredients in high-end perfumery and is a primary ingredient in Chanel No. 5. The name means 'flower of flowers' in Tagalog.
plants.traditional_uses: Flowers used in hair oil and as fragrant decorations for beds in Southeast Asian wedding traditions. The essential oil is used therapeutically in aromatherapy.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental with no significant invasive concerns in SW Florida.
